2854: Whether the Board has jurisdiction to hear preference-eligible FBI employees' whistleblower reprisal claims as an affirmative defense under 5 U.S.C. § 7701(c)(2)(C); the en banc court held it does not.
We find that the Board did not err in concluding that it lacked jurisdiction to hear FBI employees’ claims of whistleblower reprisal under § 7701(c)(2)(C).
2862: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over Brasch's USERRA appeals under 38 U.S.C. 4311(a) and 4311(b); the court held the non-frivolous allegation requirements were not met and affirmed dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
we affirm the Board's decisions dismissing his § 4311(a) claims for lack of jurisdiction.
2867: Board jurisdiction over appeal of resignation under settlement agreement; court held Board lacks jurisdiction because appellant did not make nonfrivolous allegation that resignation was involuntary.
We also agree with the Board that Ms. Robinson failed to carry her burden of establishing the Board's jurisdiction and thus affirm.
2869: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over a FERS appeal where OPM had not issued a reconsideration or initial decision and had not refused or improperly failed to decide the application.
We therefore affirm the Board's dismissal of this case for lack of jurisdiction.
2876: Government argued the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction because dependency is a fact question; court held whether a person is a statutory dependent is a question of law properly before it.
Whether a person is a dependent as defined by statute is a question of law or interpretation of law, and is properly before us.
2880: Jurisdiction over the appeal: the government argued the Little Tucker Act statute of limitations deprived the trial court of jurisdiction; the court held it had jurisdiction because the complaint was based in part on the Little Tucker Act and in part on the APA.
Moreover, we are satisfied that we have jurisdiction over Mr. Schwalier's appeal, as it is based "in whole or in part" on the Little Tucker Act.
2889: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): factual challenges to the veteran's claim (review of war-wound documentation) held outside the court's jurisdiction.
These assertions, which appear to relate only to factual issues underlying Mrs. Moffitt's claim, are outside the scope of this court's jurisdiction.
2902: Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction over tort-sounding and general civil rights claims; complaint dismissed for lack of jurisdiction

It is clear that all the claims he presents either sound in tort or amount to general allegations that his civil rights have been violated. In either case, they are outside the jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims.
2922: Mootness of the infringement suit under U.S. Patent No. 7,249,372 after the original claims were canceled in reexamination; the court found the case moot and did not reach personal jurisdiction.
Because the new patent claims added in the reexamination of the patent are not at issue in this case, we find the existing case moot for similar reasons as the companion case.
2926: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over the employee's appeal of her termination, given her status as a reemployed annuitant serving at will under 5 U.S.C. § 3323(b)(1).
Because Ms. Terrill was a reemployed annuitant and employed at will, the Board lacked jurisdiction over her appeal.
2940: Whether the district court had subject matter jurisdiction to review a Board interference decision under 35 U.S.C. § 146 after the AIA; the court held the district court lacked jurisdiction and its proceedings were a nullity.

Given that the district court did not have subject matter jurisdiction to review the Board's interference decisions, Stanford's attempt to include evidence elicited during proceedings there is inappropriate
2942: Jurisdiction of the Veterans Court: whether the May 19, 2016 Board letter was a decision reviewable under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a); court held no final decision so Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction and dismissal was proper.
Thus, because the Veterans Court did not have jurisdiction, we conclude that it properly dismissed the appeal.
2959: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over pro se complaint alleging constitutional violations; no money-mandating source identified, so no subject matter jurisdiction.
2960: Takings clause claim dismissed for lack of standing (no injury in fact) rather than a merits takings ruling.
the complaint fails to allege any "injury in fact," which is a prerequisite to establishing standing to bring a takings claim.
2961: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 to review the Veterans Court's application of equitable tolling to the facts of the case
This court does not have jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's application of the equitable tolling standard to the particular facts of this case.
2965: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over Calhoun's individual right of action appeal; no nonfrivolous allegation that protected disclosures contributed to a prohibited personnel practice, so the Board lacked jurisdiction.
Ms. Calhoun has also presented no non-frivolous allegations that the GSA's failure to promote her in 1977 justifies the Board's jurisdiction.
2967: Whether the Board has jurisdiction to enforce a settlement agreement entered in another forum; the court held it lacks statutory authority to do so.
The Board's jurisdiction is strictly limited to that provided by statute, rule, or regulation.
2972: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims: the court analyzed whether the six-year statute of limitations in § 2501 limits its jurisdiction, and held no jurisdiction over the time-barred claim.
the Court of Federal Claims correctly found that it lacked jurisdiction to hear the claim.
2979: Board jurisdiction over a challenge to a removal made under a last-chance settlement agreement; the employee failed to non-frivolously allege a knowing and voluntary agreement, performance compliance, or agency breach or bad faith, so the Board lacked jurisdiction.
Accordingly, we affirm the decision of the Merit Systems Protection Board dismissing Stovall's appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
2981: Government challenged the Court of Federal Claims' jurisdiction because SUFI bypassed the Board; court held the contracting officer's delay rendered the contractual remedy inadequate and unavailable, so SUFI could sue in the trial court.
We affirm the trial court and hold that the contracting officer's delay rendered the contractual remedy inadequate and unavailable.
2986: Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction under the Tucker Act: the court lacked jurisdiction because all of the claims sound in tort, which the Tucker Act excludes.
It is clear that all the claims she makes sound in tort. They are thus outside the jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims.
2987: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d) over the Veterans Court's application of mandamus law and its factual determinations; the court held it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed the appeal.
Because we lack jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's application of mandamus law to the facts of this case, we must dismiss Mr. Philippeaux's appeal.
3006: Jurisdiction: the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over a challenge to a civilian criminal court's jurisdiction to convict a service member.
we agree with the trial court that it lacks jurisdiction to review convictions in criminal cases
3017: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the factual finding of no present disability, the factual application of the duty to assist, the CUE application to facts, and the Board's delay, because these were factual disputes or applications of law to fact.
Unless a constitutional issue is presented, we have no jurisdiction to review questions of fact or the application of a law or regulation to a particular set of facts.
3018: Whether the two-year limitations period in 28 U.S.C. § 2636(i) is jurisdictional; held it is not, so the court need not address the limitations issue, and the CIT's jurisdiction is not defeated by the time bar.
we hold that § 2636(i) is not jurisdictional.
3019: Whether the CIT abused its discretion in declining to exercise discretionary jurisdiction to issue declaratory relief on the unliquidated and 2006 entry claims and Claim 5; held no abuse of discretion, so declaratory relief was declined.
The CIT did not abuse its discretion in declining declaratory relief.
3025: Jurisdiction: the Board lacks jurisdiction over prohibited personnel practice claims within a VEOA appeal; Bazan did not dispute this, and the court saw no error in the administrative judge's ruling and in denying discovery on those claims.
He does not dispute, however, that the Board lacks jurisdiction to hear such claims.
3028: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: court lacked jurisdiction over factual findings, application of law to facts, and constitutional claims that were constitutional in name only.
absent a constitutional issue, we lack jurisdiction to review factual findings or the application of law or regulation to the facts of a case.
3029: Appellate jurisdiction over the appeal: whether the district court properly certified a partial final judgment under Rule 54(b), so the appeal could proceed while Capital One's antitrust counterclaims remained pending.
We agree with Capital One that the district court did not abuse its discretion in certifying the appeal under Rule 54(b).
3033: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court lacks jurisdiction to review the application of law to fact in the RO's and Board's rating determinations for depression and hypertension, except for constitutional issues.

Except to the extent that an appeal presents a constitutional issue, we do not have jurisdiction to review a challenge to a factual determination or the "law or regulation as applied to the facts of a particular case."
3055: Jurisdiction limits under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's as-applied determination that the Board could properly order a medical examination, while reviewing the legal question.

And under § 7292(d)(2), we lack jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's as-applied determination, which is consistent with that standard, that the Board could properly order a medical examination here
3065: Appellate jurisdiction under AIA § 18(b)(2) over an interlocutory appeal from a denial of a motion to stay relating to CBMR petitions not yet acted on by the PTAB; court held no jurisdiction and dismissed.
For the foregoing reasons, we do not have jurisdiction under § 18(b)(2) of the AIA to consider an interlocutory appeal from a decision on a motion to stay until the PTAB institutes a CBMR proceeding.
3068: Appellate jurisdiction to review Board's §325(e)(1) estoppel determination; PTO and Westlake argued nonappealability under §324(e) and §141(c), court found jurisdiction.
We conclude that we have jurisdiction to review the CAC's estoppel argument regarding 35 U.S.C. § 325(e)(1).
3071: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over a probationary FAA excepted-service employee's appeal under 49 U.S.C. § 40122(g)(3) and the pre-April 1996 competitive-service probationary appeal regulations; the court held the Board lacked jurisdiction.
For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the Board's dismissal for want of jurisdiction.
3075: Scope of the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction to review a CAVC denial of a mandamus petition under 38 U.S.C. § 7292, including whether the denial raises a non-frivolous legal question.
We have limited jurisdiction to review decisions of the CAVC.
3082: Board jurisdiction over an appeal of an OPM reconsideration decision that OPM completely rescinded; the court held the Board lacked jurisdiction and the appeal must be dismissed.
This letter is a clear statement indicating that OPM completely rescinded its decision, thereby divesting the Board of jurisdiction.
3086: Jurisdiction over Coleman's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against the individual judges and clerk; the Tucker Act does not reach them and the United States is the only proper defendant, so the claim was insubstantial and properly dismissed.
The Court of Federal Claims cannot hear Coleman's claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 even against the United States.
3087: Jurisdiction over constitutional due process and equal protection claims; the Tucker Act reaches only money-mandating provisions and the constitutional claims are not money-mandating.
The Tucker Act limits the court's jurisdiction over constitutional claims to those arising from money-mandating provisions, and the constitutional claims brought by Coleman are not such provisions.
3088: Jurisdiction over breach of contract claims premised on filing suit and paying a filing fee; no contract with the United States was formed, so the court properly declined jurisdiction.
the mere payment of a filing fee and other litigation-related expenses does not create a contract between a plaintiff and the United States.
3090: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction under the Tucker Act over claims under the ADA, California's Unruh Civil Rights Act, and the APA because none is money-mandating; dismissal under RCFC 12(b)(1) affirmed.
we affirm the Court of Federal Claims' determination that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Pierce's case.
3100: Board jurisdiction over appeal of allegedly involuntary disability retirement (non-frivolous showing of involuntariness, coercion, and USERRA/VEOA exhaustion as jurisdictional bases); Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction affirmed.
Because Mr. Nelson failed to raise a non-frivolous claim of jurisdiction, this court affirms.
3123: Board jurisdiction over Shu's removal as a Chapter 75 adverse action: court held the Board lacked jurisdiction because Shu was not a preference-eligible, supervisory, or personnel-work postal employee under 39 U.S.C. § 1005(a)(4)(A).
Thus, the Board properly found that Mr. Shu did not have the right to challenge his removal before the Board as an adverse action appeal under Chapter 75 of Title 5.
3124: Board jurisdiction over Shu's restoration-rights claim: court held no jurisdiction because the removal was for cause substantially unrelated to his compensable injury, so no restoration rights attached under 5 C.F.R. § 353.108.
Thus, Mr. Shu has not met his burden of establishing the Board's jurisdiction over this appeal based on restoration rights.
3130: Court held it lacks jurisdiction to review the application of law to facts (claimant's combat-service argument) under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2)
To the extent that Mr. Lamm argues that the Veterans Court erred in applying this law to the facts of his case, this court does not have jurisdiction to review such questions.
3136: Jurisdiction over Fifth Amendment takings claim: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction because the takings claim was a collateral attack on bankruptcy and district court judgments.
Thus, the true nature of Ivaldy's claims is a collateral attack on the judgments of the bankruptcy court and district court. The Claims Court does not possess jurisdiction to entertain them.
3137: Jurisdiction over constitutional claims (Due Process, Privileges and Immunities, Article I uniform bankruptcy laws, separation of powers): none of the cited provisions is money-mandating, so no Tucker Act jurisdiction.
Because Ivaldy's claims are not tied to money-mandating sources of law, the Claims Court does not possess jurisdiction to entertain them.
3141: Jurisdiction: the court held it lacks subject matter jurisdiction over appeal 2015-1959 from the District of Arizona, which involves Title VII and related employment discrimination claims, and affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal in appeal 2015-5142 for lack of jurisdiction over Title VII discrimination claims.
This court is a court of limited jurisdiction, which does not include appeals of district court orders involving the kind of allegations proffered in Mr. Haque's Amended Complaint.
3155: Jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court: court lacks jurisdiction because appellant challenges factual finding and application of law to facts rather than a rule of law or statute interpretation under 38 U.S.C. § 7292.

Because Mr. Gaeta is actually challenging the Veterans Court's factual finding that the evidence of record was adequate to rebut the presumption of soundness. Because we may not review a challenge to a factual determination or a challenge to the application of law to facts, see 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), we dismiss Mr. Gaeta's appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
3156: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court dismissed the appeal of the Veterans Court's final denial of a non-service-connected pension for lack of jurisdiction because the appellant challenged only factual findings and the application of law to fact; remanded service-connection claims were not reviewable as non-final.

Nonetheless, because Mr. Smithers only challenges fact findings or the application of law to fact, we lack jurisdiction over the appeal of the Veterans Court's denial of the claim for a non-service-connected pension under § 7292.
3172: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over CAVC review: no jurisdiction to review factual determinations or application of law to facts absent a constitutional question.
Absent a constitutional question, we do not possess jurisdiction to review any challenge to a factual determination or the application of a law or regulation to the facts of a particular case.
3176: Pendent appellate jurisdiction over the stay decision alongside the appealable denial of a preliminary injunction; court analyzed whether to exercise jurisdiction over the stay order.

Considering that the district court in this case maintained the stay and denied the preliminary injunction concurrently in a single order, those decisions are inextricably linked and we exercise our discretion to consider the district court's stay decision along with its denial of a preliminary injunction.
3182: Mootness of the companion appeal: the court found this IPR appeal moot in light of its contemporaneous holding that the challenged patents claim ineligible subject matter under §101, dismissed the appeal, and vacated the Board's decisions.
In light of our decision in Chicago Bd. Options Exch., Inc. v. Int'l Secs. Exch., ... we find this companion case moot. We dismiss the appeal and vacate the Board's decisions.
3188: Federal Circuit jurisdiction to review a Veterans Court mandamus denial under 38 U.S.C. 7292; the government contested jurisdiction and the court held it has jurisdiction to review a non-frivolous legal question, but not factual merits.
we do have jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's "decision whether to grant a mandamus petition that raises a non-frivolous legal question."
3195: Appellate jurisdiction over the district court's order granting a new trial on damages; no jurisdiction because no final decision on damages, Rule 54(b) and section 1292(c)(2) do not apply.
we lack jurisdiction to consider whether the court erred in ordering a new trial on damages.
3198: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. §7292: veteran's challenge to the Board's factual finding on veteran status/period of war (pension claim) is not reviewable, so the appeal is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Ms. Nails' challenge thus requires us to evaluate the Board's factual finding or at most application of law to the facts, to which we lack jurisdiction.
3199: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction over the depression claim because the Board never decided it; Federal Circuit affirms that dismissal under 38 U.S.C. §7252 and Howard v. Gober.
Because Ms. Nails had not appealed the RO's 2014 decision on her depression claim to the Board, the Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction over her depression claim.
3200: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a) to review the overpayment (waiver of $8,857 recovery) issue because it was not properly on appeal; Federal Circuit affirmed.
We find that the Veterans Court correctly found that it lacked jurisdiction under § 7252(a) because the Board decision on review before the Veterans Court did not cover the overpayment issue
3201: Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) to review the Veterans Court's application of 38 C.F.R. § 3.400(o)(2) to the facts (earlier effective date for TDIU), and the Veterans Court's waiver/abandonment ruling is not within its jurisdiction.
We lack jurisdiction over such a challenge.
3219: Board jurisdiction over the claim based on an anonymous complaint to the Alabama Board of Nursing: the court held no error in excluding it because such a complaint is not a personnel action under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(a)(2).

We see no error in the Board's decision to exclude Ms. Griesbach's claim based on the anonymous complaint because, as the AJ noted in the order closing the record, such a complaint is not a personnel action as defined by 5 U.S.C. § 2302(a)(2).
3230: Whether the MSPB had authority to review FEMA's feasibility of transferring Ryan to a nonsensitive position. The court held the MSPB lacked authority to review it because the position required a clearance.
The MSPB is therefore not authorized to review FEMA's determination with respect to the feasibility of Ms. Ryan's transfer to an alternative position
3231: Whether the MSPB could order restoration or review the post-acquittal indefinite suspension and the delay in the clearance determination. The court held the MSPB correctly declined to order restoration to a position requiring a clearance.
The MSPB correctly held it is without authority to order the agency to return an uncleared employee to a position that requires a security clearance.
3235: Mootness: appeal dismissed as moot because the related DISH Network appeal affirmed invalidity of the same claims, so no live controversy remained
Accordingly, we dismiss this appeal as moot.
3241: Count II: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction because no source of law (25 U.S.C. § 396) supplies the specific fiduciary duty to disclose information during Cobell settlement proceedings
Appellants' Count II fails at the first hurdle.
3243: Jurisdiction and mootness: the Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review the factual challenge to the Delgado declaration under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2), and the CAVC's dismissal of the mandamus petition as moot was appropriate because the relief had been accomplished.
By statute, we do not have jurisdiction to review the factual details of the claims before the RO and the BVA, unless constitutional aspects are implicated.
3248: Appellate jurisdiction: the court held no Article III case or controversy remained after the settlement, so it dismissed the appeal from the sanctions order for lack of jurisdiction.

Because we find that, in light of the settlement entered by all parties to the litigation, including the Attorneys, there remains no on-going case or controversy, we dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
3250: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over Baseden's alleged reduction-in-pay appeal, which turned on whether he was an 'employee' under 5 U.S.C. § 7511 (probationer, applicant, or reinstated employee).
We agree with the Board that Mr. Baseden is not an employee within the meaning of 5 U.S.C. § 7511 and affirm its final decision dismissing the matter.
3265: No Board jurisdiction over the separation claims (precluded) and over the VEOA claim, which cannot reach pre-enactment events.
Therefore, we agree with the Board’s determination of no jurisdiction.
3267: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over a removal appeal after the employee signed a settlement agreement waiving appeal rights, including whether the agreement was voluntarily executed.
Mr. Vaughan has not demonstrated that the Board had jurisdiction to hear his appeal or otherwise committed legal error in its decision, we affirm.
3273: Justiciability: merits of the Navy's decision to disenroll Kennedy from OCS and NROTC were not justiciable, while statutory and regulatory challenges were reviewable
the Court of Federal Claims correctly held that the adjudication of those merits were not justiciable, because the decision pertained to who should be permitted to serve in the Marine Corps
3278: Mootness: Claims Court dismissed Guardian's First Post-Award Protest as moot because the agency's corrective action gave the relief sought; affirmed.
Accordingly, we affirm the Claims Court's determination that the corrective action moots Guardian's First Post-Award Protest.
3283: MSPB jurisdiction over Hill's fourteen-day suspension appeal; the Board dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because a suspension of more than fourteen days is required under 5 U.S.C. § 7512, and the court affirmed.
we affirm the Board's decision dismissing the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, as Mr. Hill's suspension was for only fourteen days.
3294: Jurisdiction under the Tucker Act: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over contract claims because plaintiff was not a party or third-party beneficiary, and over tort claims which are excluded from Tucker Act jurisdiction.
Accordingly, the Court of Federal Claims correctly found that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Ogunniyi's contract claims.
3303: Appellate jurisdiction over the Veterans Court's denial of Belton's motions for sanctions and to compel production; the court held it lacked jurisdiction because those rulings rested on application of law to facts.

to the extent Mr. Belton appeals from the Veterans Court's decisions on his motions for sanctions and to compel production, we lack jurisdiction over those matters because those decisions rest on the Veterans Court's application of law to the facts.
3322: Jurisdiction: whether the Board had jurisdiction over the appeal, which turned on whether Thomas's FAA retirement was involuntary; the Board dismissed for lack of jurisdiction after finding the retirement voluntary, and the court affirmed.
The AJ dismissed Ms. Thomas' case for lack of jurisdiction, on the basis that the retirement was voluntary.
3324: Appellate jurisdiction: the court held it lacks jurisdiction over a petition for review not filed within the 60-day period of 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A), treating that deadline as jurisdictional and dismissing.
Accordingly, this court lacks jurisdiction over petitions for review that fail to comply with the requirements of § 7703(b)(1)(A).
3330: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court denial of mandamus-type extraordinary relief; the court held that it lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2) because the appellant challenged only factual determinations and the application of law to facts.
For the reasons stated above we find that we are without jurisdiction to consider this appeal and must therefore dismiss this case.
3344: Board jurisdiction over the termination appeal: whether Turner was an 'employee' under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1)(A) (completed probation or one year of continuous service), which the Board found lacking, leading to dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
Because it is undisputed that the agency terminated Mr. Turner effective January 23, 2015, Mr. Turner did not complete his one-year probationary period or his one year of current continuous service.
3351: Board jurisdiction over the termination appeal: the Board lacked jurisdiction because Hernandez did not complete one year of current continuous service under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1)(B), and military service could not be added to civilian service; the race discrimination claim fell with the lack of jurisdiction over the agency action.
Since the Board lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Hernandez's agency action, it did not have jurisdiction over his race discrimination claim.
3352: Appellate jurisdiction over an appeal from a Veterans Court remand order; the court held the remand was not a final decision and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction under the Williams finality exception test.
Because all of the conditions are not satisfied, we cannot "depart from the strict rule of finality" and, thus, do not have jurisdiction to adjudicate Mr. Flores-Vazquez's appeal.
3363: Jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over correction of military records, which is not incident of and collateral to a money judgment once the back pay claim is time-barred.

Because the Claims Court lacked jurisdiction over Jackson’s claim for back pay due to the time bar, it also correctly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction over his claim for correction of his military records.
3364: Jurisdiction: no Tucker Act jurisdiction over tort, defamation-based punitive damages, or breach of contract claims.
Thus, Jackson’s claim for punitive damages based on defamation of character, libel, and slander is outside of the Claim’s Court’s jurisdiction.
3365: Jurisdiction: disability retirement pay claim not within jurisdiction because the claim has not accrued, as administrative remedies before the proper board were not exhausted.
Thus, the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over that claim.
3368: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 to review the Veterans Court's dismissal for lack of a final Board decision; court held it lacked jurisdiction because the challenge was factual or an application of law to facts.
Because we also lack jurisdiction, we dismiss.
3376: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has Tucker Act jurisdiction over the breach of settlement agreement claim, or whether the Medicare Act preempts it and the claim arises under the Medicare Act. Held the CFC has exclusive jurisdiction; transfer of this claim affirmed.
We hold that the Court of Federal Claims has exclusive jurisdiction under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1491, over Prime Hospitals' breach of contract claim
3377: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction over the alternative declaratory, injunctive and mandamus claims. Held it lacks jurisdiction; transfer of those claims reversed.

We conclude that the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Prime Hospitals' remaining claims and we reverse the district court's order transferring Prime Hospitals' claims for declaratory, injunctive, and mandamus relief.
3378: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292: factual challenges to the Veterans Court's mandamus ruling (ignoring facts, misapplying facts) are beyond review, while legal error in interpreting mandamus law is reviewable.
Thus, with regard to Mr. Bauer's arguments that the Veterans Court "ignor[ed] the facts of the case," ... such arguments are beyond this court's jurisdiction.
3381: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction because the Board remanded the disability rating claim, and a Board remand is not a decision under 38 U.S.C. 7252(a).
the Veterans Court was required by statute, as interpreted by Kirkpatrick, to dismiss Mr. Gaines's appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
3388: Appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1295(a)(1): the parties disputed jurisdiction, and the court found jurisdiction based on compulsory counterclaim 5 (VCPA preempted by patent law), which arises under the patent laws under Gunn.
Because we find jurisdiction on the basis of at least one of MPHJ's counterclaims, counterclaim 5, we have jurisdiction over this appeal.
3398: Appellate jurisdiction: the court lacks jurisdiction to review the October 27, 2015 summary judgment/dismissal order because the notice of appeal was untimely and identified only the December 30, 2015 reconsideration order.
We therefore lack jurisdiction to review the October 27, 2015 order.
3411: Whether the FDIC's revocation of an accepted term-extension offer was a removal under 5 U.S.C. § 7512, which determined whether the Federal Circuit had jurisdiction over the arbitration appeal; the court held no jurisdiction and dismissed.
Thus, this court lacks jurisdiction over Mr. Reddick's appeal. Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.
3416: Court held that challenges to the Board's weighing of evidence and credibility determinations, and an unsupported due process assertion, are outside its jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(c).
These issues are outside our jurisdiction. See 38 U.S.C. § 7292(c); King v. Shinseki, 700 F.3d 1339, 1345–46 (Fed. Cir. 2012)
3429: Whether the Board had statutory authority to review the '191 patent as a covered business method patent under AIA section 18; the court held the patent is outside the CBM definition, so the Board lacked authority.
We draw the same conclusion here, and further conclude that the patent at issue is outside the definition of a CBM patent that Congress provided by statute.
3435: Tucker Act jurisdiction over Title VII discrimination claim: Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction because Title VII provides an exclusive, comprehensive scheme.
The Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Mr. Baker's Title VII discrimination claim.
3436: Tucker Act jurisdiction over tort claims (defamation, emotional distress, retaliation): tort claims fall outside the Tucker Act's grant because it excludes claims sounding in tort.
Therefore, the Court of Federal Claims correctly held that it lacks jurisdiction over Mr. Baker's tort claims.
3437: Tucker Act jurisdiction over wrongful garnishment of tax refund under the Debt Collection Improvement Act: the statute does not mandate monetary relief.

The statutory provisions relied on by Mr. Baker authorize an agency to withhold funds payable by the United States to a person to satisfy a claim, but they do not authorize monetary relief for a violation.
3438: Tucker Act jurisdiction over breach-of-settlement-agreement contract claim: the claim is money-mandating under Holmes and Cunningham, so the Court of Federal Claims erred in dismissing for lack of jurisdiction.
The Court of Federal Claims therefore erred in holding that it lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction over Mr. Baker's contract claim.
3444: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over the tax refund suit, barred by 26 U.S.C. § 6512(a) because the taxpayer previously petitioned the Tax Court for the same taxable year.
We agree with the government that the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over Widtfeldt's complaint.
3445: Jurisdiction over claims against nonsovereign defendants (Settlement Officer Murphy, Treasury, Commissioner of Internal Revenue), which is limited to claims against the United States.
Moreover, we discern no error in the Claims Court's dismissal of the nonsovereign defendants from this action, or its dismissal of the remaining allegations as frivolous.
3448: MSPB jurisdiction over partially recovered employee's restoration claim; employee failed to make nonfrivolous allegations of arbitrary and capricious denial, so dismissal for lack of jurisdiction was affirmed.
These four statements, however, do not present any specific facts or plausible assertions that would prove the USPS acted arbitrarily or capriciously towards Ms. Clark.
3452: Mootness of the removal appeal; the Board lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the appeal after the agency rescinded the removal, and the appeal was dismissed as moot.
Accordingly, we agree with the Board that Holleman's appeal was rendered moot and thus dismissal was appropriate.
3459: Veterans Court authority to issue declaratory judgments: the court held the Veterans Court is not a court of the United States under 28 U.S.C. 2201 and properly denied the petition as outside its authority.
Accordingly, the Veterans Court properly denied Ms. Michael's petition for declaratory judgment as not within the scope of its authority.
3460: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1295 and 38 U.S.C. 7292 to review the district court, Fifth Circuit and Supreme Court decisions dismissing the FTCA complaints: no basis for review was alleged or exists.
Regardless of the substance of her arguments, Ms. Michael does not allege any of the limited bases on which this court would have jurisdiction to review the decision of the district court.
3461: Mootness: the court dismissed the appeal as moot because a grievance settlement awarding full back pay and benefits resolved the controversy, leaving no live case or controversy.
Mr. Campbell's response has not established any remaining controversy. Accordingly, this appeal is DISMISSED No costs.
3476: Appellate jurisdiction: court dismissed appeal because the claims raised were purely factual and outside 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) review limits.
We dismiss the appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction.
3484: Mootness of appeal from denial of preliminary injunction, which was sought only until the district court decided the judgment-on-the-pleadings motions
Amgen's appeal from the denial of a preliminary injunction is moot. We therefore dismiss that aspect of Amgen's appeal.
3486: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 over the Veterans Court's dismissal of a Notice of Appeal as untimely; court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the application of equitable tolling to the facts.
Because Mr. Harrington has not raised any issue within our limited jurisdiction, we must dismiss his appeal.
3494: Appeals from the -1278 and -1282 decisions as to claims already held unpatentable in the companion IPR were dismissed as moot.
We therefore dismiss as moot Securus’s challenge to the Board’s analysis of these claims in the -1282 IPR Board Decision.
3496: Whether the district court had subject matter jurisdiction to review the PTAB's decision to institute CBM review; held barred by 35 U.S.C. § 324(e).
the district court was correct in barring judicial review pursuant to subsection 324(e).
3505: Jurisdiction over constitutional challenges to MSPB administrative judge decision despite § 713(e)(2) finality language; intervenors contested jurisdiction and the court held it has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) and 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1).
Accordingly, we have jurisdiction over Ms. Helman's constitutional claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1).
3520: Jurisdiction limits under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: no jurisdiction over the remand of the right knee increased-rating claim (not a final decision), or over the effect of the back condition on quality of life, or over the weighing of evidence (factual determinations).
We conclude that we lack jurisdiction to consider Diamond's first argument.
3526: Mootness of the claimant's cross-appeal on whether the full 2,273 days of incarceration are compensable, after the court reversed on the government's appeal.
Mr. Crooker's cross-appeal is therefore moot.
3531: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction to review Board's remand decision (not a final appealable decision under 38 U.S.C. 7252(a)); Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal and dismissed remaining portions for lack of jurisdiction over denials of stay extension and reassignment as factual determinations outside 7292 review
Because the Veterans Court correctly determined that it lacked jurisdiction to review the Board's remand decision, we affirm that portion of the Veterans Court's decision.
3538: Jurisdiction over a petition filed before the MSPB initial decision became final; the Government contested jurisdiction and the court held it had jurisdiction under Schmitt and Graves.
We conclude that we have jurisdiction over Mr. Jones's appeal and that the AJ properly denied his claims.
3552: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over Veterans Court appeal under 38 U.S.C. § 7292; court lacked jurisdiction over factual and application-of-law challenges to 1986 CUE decision and rating classification
Because we lack subject matter jurisdiction over the issues that Mr. Sudranski raises, we dismiss.
3556: Jurisdiction: lack of privity between GIT (subcontractor) and the government, so the court lacked jurisdiction over Counts I-III brought in GIT's own name.
We therefore agree with the Court of Federal Claims that privity, and thus jurisdiction, is lacking as to GIT's Counts I-III brought in its own name against the government.
3561: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292: a constitutional label alone does not confer jurisdiction over the due process challenge to alleged record tampering, which the court found was not a non-frivolous constitutional issue.
Merely characterizing a claim as constitutional is not enough, however, to 'confer upon us jurisdiction that we otherwise lack.'
3564: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 over a Veterans Court affirmance of Board credibility findings; the court held credibility and weighing of evidence are factual, and a due process challenge was constitutional in name only, so it dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
We dismiss Burnley's appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
3570: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over an appeal by a reemployed annuitant terminated at will; the MSPB dismissed for lack of jurisdiction and the Federal Circuit affirmed.
we agree with the MSPB that there is no basis on which to find jurisdiction in this case, merely from the administrative judge's willingness to hold a jurisdictional hearing in a previous case.
3571: Jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction because no money-mandating source of law was identified, tort and diversity bases were excluded, and the false imprisonment claim was not viable.
We conclude that the Claims Court correctly determined that it lacked jurisdiction over Ms. Barber's appeal.
3577: Finality and appellate jurisdiction: whether the judgment was final although Prism's '288 patent claims were abandoned without a separate dismissal order.
3578: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over Jones's qui tam-based money claims and related contract and Bivens theories; the court held the Claims Court lacked jurisdiction.
The Claims Court correctly concluded it was without jurisdiction to consider Mr. Jones’s claims.
3586: Court of Federal Claims lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint contained no non-frivolous allegation of an enforceable contract with an arbitration clause; dismissal affirmed.
the Claims Court granted the government's motion to dismiss on the ground that it had no subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint contained no non-frivolous allegation.
3594: Jurisdiction: scope of Federal Circuit review of the Veterans Court's discretionary issue exhaustion decision; court held it has jurisdiction over the pure legal question of the doctrine's scope but not over application of law to fact.
But to the extent that the issue raised involves solely a legal interpretation, we possess jurisdiction.
3607: Tucker Act jurisdiction over breach of settlement agreement claim; government argued the settlement disavowed money damages, and the court held jurisdiction proper.
Thus, jurisdiction was proper in the Court of Federal Claims pursuant to the Tucker Act.
3627: Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) because the appeal challenged factual determinations and application of law to facts; appeal dismissed.

Because Mr. Shuler's appeal of the Veterans Court's decision only involves factual determinations and the application of law to the facts of the case, Mr. Shuler's appeal is beyond the scope of our jurisdiction.
3628: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over tort damages claim and requested injunction under the Tucker Act; dismissal affirmed.
Because we agree that the Court of Federal Claims does not have jurisdiction over Mr. Champion's tort claims, we affirm.
3629: Appellate jurisdiction under 9 U.S.C. 16(a)(1)(B) over the denial of the section 4 motion to compel arbitration; court held the ruling on arbitrability would be advisory and declined to entertain that part of the appeal.
We will not entertain the appeal insofar as it involves the denial of an order to compel arbitration under § 4.
3630: Appellate jurisdiction under 9 U.S.C. 16(a)(1)(A) over an asserted refusal of a section 3 stay; court held the January 28 Order contained no appealable refusal of a stay.
The district court's January 28 Order does not include an order refusing a stay that is appealable under 9 U.S.C. § 16(a)(1)(A).
3635: Commission lacked jurisdiction under Section 337 because electronically transmitted digital data is not an 'article' of importation; court reversed and remanded for lack of jurisdiction.
Accordingly, we reverse and remand the Commission's decision and conclude that the Commission does not have jurisdiction over this case.
3640: Board dismissed the restoration appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Barton could not prove a compensable injury; the court held the Board properly determined it lacked jurisdiction.

We hold that the Board properly determined it lacked jurisdiction on the basis that Mr. Barton was unable to show by a preponderance of evidence that he was separated as a result of a compensable injury.
3641: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over Morales's appeal of his restoration after OWCP benefits; the Board dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the claimed benefits were not within 5 U.S.C. § 8151(a), and the court affirmed.
We agree with the Board that Mr. Morales has failed to meet his burden.
3653: Board lacked jurisdiction over the IRA appeal because the alleged protected disclosures were not nonfrivolous and the personnel actions predated the only protected disclosure; the court affirmed the dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
The Board properly dismissed Mr. El's IRA appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Mr. El's disclosures described only a vague allegation of wrongdoing and were not protected.
3657: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction over Grayton's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim; the Veterans Court's jurisdiction is limited to Board decisions.
The Veterans Court therefore correctly concluded that an action under § 1983 is a civil action over which it lacks jurisdiction.
3658: Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over FTCA, Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment claims that were not raised in or addressed by the Veterans Court.
We lack jurisdiction to consider claims neither addressed by the Veterans Court nor raised by a party to the Veterans Court.
3659: Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) to review the breach-of-contract or IEP claims, which were construed as challenges to the Board's application of regulations and adequacy of reasons or bases.
We lack jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court decision under either interpretation.
3670: Court of Federal Claims lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the amended complaint against the United States was not based on a money-mandating source of law and sounded in tort or criminal law.
Mr. Upshaw's claims are based on criminal law or tort. The Claims Court does not have jurisdiction over such claims.
3673: Personal jurisdiction over the accused patentee in a declaratory judgment action; court held no specific personal jurisdiction over Anser
We agree with the district court that it lacked specific personal jurisdiction over Anser.
3677: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction over constitutional, statutory, criminal-statute, and regulatory claims because those provisions are not money-mandating

The Court of Federal Claims correctly concluded it lacked jurisdiction to decide the majority of Mr. Harris's claims because the relevant constitutional, statutory, and regulatory provisions are not money mandating.
3689: Mootness: the appeal from the -6122 Board decision was dismissed as moot because the -4281 decision covered the same claims.
We, therefore, dismiss as moot Affinity’s appeal of the -6122 Board Decision upholding the unpatentability of a subset of claims affirmed as unpatentable in the -4281 Board Decision.
3717: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction to review Avalos's removal, given the government's argument that his appointment was invalid and that he had not completed a probationary year; the court held the Board had jurisdiction because Avalos had more than one year of current continuous federal civilian service.
As a result, Mr. Avalos had the right to appeal his removal to the Board; the Board had the jurisdiction to review it.
3729: Jurisdiction: Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over Fourth Amendment fraudulent assessment and taking claims because they sound in tort under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1).
The Claims Court also lacks jurisdiction over Fourth Amendment fraudulent assessment and fraudulent taking claims because they are actions allegedly "grounded upon fraud" that "sound in tort."
3750: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over the Chapter 75 removal appeal, given the administrative judge's dismissal under the election requirement of 5 C.F.R. § 1209.2(d), which the court held inapplicable because the petitioner was a supervisor and not an 'employee.'
The administrative judge erred in interpreting 5 C.F.R. § 1209.2(d), which applies only to employees, as applying to Ms. Kammunkun, who was a supervisor.
3755: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 over the Veterans Court decision; the appeal challenged only factual determinations and application of law to facts, so the court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
We lack jurisdiction to review those challenges.
3759: Subject matter jurisdiction of the district court over the underlying case, as decided in the companion appeal 2018-1616, which resulted in vacatur of the fee judgment.

Based on our holding in Inspired Development Group, LLC v. Inspired Products Group, LLC, 2018-1616 (Fed. Cir. Sept. 18, 2019), that the district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the case underlying that appeal and this appeal, we vacate the district court’s judgment awarding attorneys’ fees.
3770: Jurisdiction over the Miltons' contract claims: the Claims Court lacked jurisdiction because neither the Miltons nor (via third-party beneficiary theory) the Miltons were parties to the contract with privity; the Tucker Act requires privity.
Accordingly, we affirm the Claims Court's holding that it does not have jurisdiction over the Miltons' contract claims.
3787: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over Section 1110 disability benefits, military pay under 37 U.S.C. 204, and FTCA tort claims, contested on the government's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1).
The Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction to hear a claim for benefits under Section 1110 or comparable Title 38 provisions.
3794: Appeals in IPR2018-00017 and IPR2018-00366 dismissed as moot because all claims on appeal were held invalid in IPR2018-00096.
Having held that all claims on appeal are invalid, we dismiss the appeals in IPR2018-00017 and IPR2018-00366 as moot.
3795: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over Hitsman's claims that the IRS unlawfully seized assets, including Fourth Amendment and Fifth/Fourteenth Amendment due process theories, which the court held are not money-mandating under the Tucker Act.
Because the Court of Federal Claims lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over Mr. Hitsman's claim, we affirm.
3797: Jurisdiction over discharge of student loans: CFC lacks Tucker Act jurisdiction to discharge debt; affirmed dismissal of that claim.
We agree that the Court of Federal Claims did not have jurisdiction over plaintiff's claims for discharge of her student loan.
3798: Jurisdiction over illegal exaction claim: CFC erred in holding it lacked jurisdiction over the exaction claim.
We find that the trial court erred in dismissing the claim.
3802: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over tax-based, tort, and due process claims; dismissal under Rule 12(b)(1) affirmed for lack of jurisdiction

Because Taylor has failed to allege any claim that falls within the Claims Court's jurisdiction, the Claims Court was correct in dismissing her complaint under Rule 12(b)(1) of the Rules of the United States Court of Federal Claims.
3804: Section 1500 jurisdictional bar: whether the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction because the claim was for or in respect to claims pending in another court (Third Circuit appeal and District Court suit).
Because we find that the two cases are not "for or in respect to" the same claims, we reverse the Claims Court's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction and remand for further proceedings.
3817: Jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1500: the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over the transferred Equal Pay Act claim because the same claim was pending in the Central District of California against the United States.
Therefore, § 1500 applies, the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Mr. Philbert's Equal Pay Act claim, and his complaint was correctly dismissed.
3824: Jurisdiction: government argued the Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction because the Veterans Court's alternative holding was a factual finding; court rejected the objection and reached the legal question under 38 U.S.C. § 7292.
3827: Whether the Court of International Trade had jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(a) over the protest denials, including whether Customs' protest decisions were 'decisions' that could be protested under 19 U.S.C. § 1514(a) and not merely ministerial actions.
We therefore hold that the Court of International Trade had jurisdiction in this matter under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(a).
3830: Vacatur of the merits judgment on the alternative § 1581(i) claim, which the court found had nothing left to decide once § 1581(a) jurisdiction was established.
It follows that there is nothing to decide on the second claim. Accordingly, we vacate the merits judgment on that claim.
3845: Jurisdiction: the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over the regulatory takings claim because it was not ripe, since the Inholders never applied for a special use permit.
The Court of Federal Claims is without jurisdiction to consider takings claims that are not ripe.
3852: Jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court: court lacks jurisdiction to review factual determinations, application of law to facts, challenges to pending remand issues, and abandonment rulings under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2).
Therefore, we lack jurisdiction over Mr. Payne's challenges and dismiss this appeal.
3854: Jurisdiction: whether the Federal Circuit had jurisdiction over the petition for review of the arbitrator's decision, given the 60-day limit in 5 U.S.C. 7703(b)(1) treated as jurisdictional; petition dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Accordingly, this petition for review is dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
3866: Board jurisdiction: the Board lacked jurisdiction over a separate hostile work environment claim because it was not raised before OSC.
The Board thus lacked jurisdiction over a separate hostile work environment claim. 5 U.S.C. § 1214(a)(3); see Ward, 981 F.2d at 526.
3882: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court dismissed because the challenged effective-date, CUE and RO claim-interpretation questions are factual or were not properly before the court, outside its jurisdiction to review.
Because Mr. Sperlazza's appeal involves issues that fall outside this court's jurisdiction, we dismiss.
3903: Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 1985, 1986), constitutional, and RICO claims; dismissed under RCFC 12(b)(1).
The Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over claims under the Civil Rights Act, including provisions 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985 and 1986.
3914: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's affirmance of the Board's no-CUE finding on the pending-claim and fraudulent-concealment questions, which it treated as factual determinations or applications of law to fact.
Because we lack jurisdiction, we dismiss.
3918: Whether the Veterans Court had jurisdiction under Andre v. Principi to decide a CUE claim that was allegedly distinct from the CUE allegations raised before the Board. The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded for the Veterans Court to decide jurisdiction in the first instance, without deciding it.
Because the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims did not consider whether it lacked jurisdiction, we vacate and remand.
3931: Limits on Veterans Court and Federal Circuit review under 38 U.S.C. 7292: no jurisdiction over an interpretation issue that the Veterans Court did not actually decide.
We have no jurisdiction over an issue of interpretation that does not exist.
3932: Lack of jurisdiction to review the Board's factual determinations, including its weighing of Green's lay statements against medical evidence.
As explained above, we lack jurisdiction to review challenges to the Board’s factual determinations.
3938: Claims Court jurisdiction under the Tucker Act: the court held the complaint failed to identify a money-mandating provision and affirmed dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
The Claims Court properly dismissed Mr. Taebel's complaint for lack of jurisdiction.
3952: Court analyzed its jurisdiction over an appeal from partial IPR institution after SAS Institute, finding jurisdiction because no party requested SAS-based relief.
In accordance with our precedent, we conclude that we have jurisdiction over Nobel's appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(4)(A) and are not obliged to reopen non-instituted claims or grounds.
3956: Appellate jurisdiction: the court held there was no final decision because the judgment entered at Adobe's request did not finally resolve Adobe's breach of contract claim, and it dismissed both the appeal and the cross-appeal, including the denial of §285 fees and Rule 11 sanctions as unappealable interim orders.
Because there was no final decision on the merits, we dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
3960: Jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction over the due process claims, and the Federal Circuit found it lacked jurisdiction over the appeal.
we agree that the Claims Court lacked jurisdiction over Sanders' complaint and find that we lack jurisdiction over his appeal.
3964: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over Donnelly's Federal Tort Claims Act-type tort claims for lost mail; court held tort claims are excluded from Tucker Act jurisdiction and no money-mandating source identified.
Because the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction to consider tort claims, the court properly dismissed Donnelly's complaint.
3972: Declaratory-judgment jurisdiction: the court held the district court erred in finding no case or controversy based on infringement, but affirmed dismissal because the declaratory invalidity claim would not resolve the contractual dispute and no other pending litigation would resolve it, so no jurisdiction exists over the invalidity question.
Without taking at least that step, in either the American or British courts, it cannot establish declaratory-judgment jurisdiction over the question of invalidity.
3986: Lack of jurisdiction over the request to correct military records, because the equitable relief was not incident to a money judgment under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(2).
Because the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over any claims for monetary relief, it correctly held that it also lacked jurisdiction over this claim for equitable relief.
3987: Lack of jurisdiction over the APA, Eighth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, enlistment, promissory estoppel and misrepresentation claims because they are not money-mandating sources of law within the Tucker Act.
it is well established that the Court of Federal Claims does not have jurisdiction over such claims.
4016: Scope of the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292, where the court analyzed whether the appeal presented a reviewable question of law rather than a challenge to facts or application of law to facts.
because it is undisputed that Scott suffers from an unlisted service-connected foot condition, we have jurisdiction.
4017: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over Veterans Court review of CUE pleading dismissal, service connection presumption, and other arguments; court held it lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) because the issues were factual or application of law to fact.
Because we lack jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's decision, we dismiss this appeal.
4019: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court lacked jurisdiction over the CUE challenge because it presented a factual or application-of-law-to-fact question, not a legal interpretation or constitutional claim, so the appeal was dismissed.
But that challenge is outside our limited jurisdiction: it does not involve a dispute about the interpretation of a law or regulation or a constitutional claim.
4020: Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over Goforth's constitutional claims (First, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments) because those provisions are not money-mandating under the Tucker Act.
These constitutional provisions that Ms. Goforth alleges were violated are not money mandating and are therefore outside the limited jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims.
4031: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292: the Secretary contested jurisdiction, and the court held it could review the legal question because no factual findings precluded review.
These are questions of law, and we therefore may exercise jurisdiction to review this challenge under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a).
4064: Appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1295(a)(1): the Agreed Final Judgment is final only as to Microsoft; the court lacks jurisdiction over the ruling as it extends to the Manufacturer defendants and their §287 notice.

Therefore, we affirm the district court's decision only to the extent it held that Iron Oak did not provide sufficient notice under 35 U.S.C. § 287 to Microsoft. But to the extent the district court's final judgment purports to extend beyond the only defendant in this case, Microsoft, and to the sufficiency of notice under § 287 to defendants outside of this case, we do not have jurisdiction.
4077: Mootness: the appeal from the denial of preliminary injunctive relief against a CICA stay override became moot after the stay expired, and the 'capable of repetition, yet evading review' exception does not apply.
Because the stay has since expired, we dismiss Safeguard's appeal as moot.
4078: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction over challenges to the weight of evidence, the merits of factual findings, and the application of law to facts (including effective-date, § 5110, § 4.2 and § 7104(a) review arguments), and reviewed only the legal challenge.
Absent a constitutional violation, however, we have no jurisdiction to review factual determinations or the application of law to facts.
4080: Board jurisdiction: whether petitioners qualified as 'employees' with appeal rights under 5 U.S.C. 7511(a)(1)(B)(ii) given breaks in service, so the Board lacked jurisdiction over their removal appeals; court affirmed dismissal under OPM's continuous-service regulation.
Because we agree with the Board's interpretation of § 7511, we affirm its dismissal of Mr. Williams's and Mr. Winns's respective cases.
4081: Whether Williams retained Board appeal rights from his prior RCA position under the Exum rule when the agency failed to advise him of the loss of appeal rights; court rejected Exum and held no retained jurisdiction.
We hold that the agency's failure to advise Mr. Williams does not allow him to retain appeal rights from a prior appointment.
4084: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over Brennecke's tax-related and tort-type claims; court held he failed to establish jurisdiction, including no allegation of paid assessed taxes or timely IRS refund claim.
As the court correctly determined, Brennecke failed to establish that it had jurisdiction to consider his claim.
4088: Federal Circuit jurisdiction limited by 38 U.S.C. § 7292: court lacks jurisdiction to review factual determination of fraud, application of 38 C.F.R. § 3.343 to facts, and the CUE challenge to the 1986 rating decision that the Board did not address; conclusory constitutional assertions insufficient to invoke jurisdiction.
We conclude that we lack jurisdiction to review any of the issues raised by Mr. Morris.
4089: Whether the Court of Federal Claims had jurisdiction to award guardianship-maintenance expenses under 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-15(a) after the merits judgment became final and unappealed. The court held the CFC lacked jurisdiction because the merits judgment was final.
The Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction to grant Ms. McCulloch the guardianship fees under § 300aa-15(a).
4100: Scope of the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court held it cannot review the factual determinations challenged by the veteran, leaving only legal questions.
All other conclusions Mr. Cones challenges on appeal are factual and outside the scope of our jurisdiction.
4101: Appellate jurisdiction: the court analyzed whether it could hear a constitutional challenge to a federal retirement statute, given the statutory limits on review of MSPB decisions, and found jurisdiction.
We have authority to consider Hirschfield's claim that section 8418 is unconstitutional.
4115: Constitutional challenge to inter partes review is moot after Oil States

Prior to the Supreme Court's decision in Oil States Energy Servs., LLC v. Green's Energy Grp., LLC, 138 S. Ct. 1365 (2018), VirnetX argued we should wait for the Supreme Court to decide whether inter partes review is constitutional. That issue is now moot.
4121: Whether a prima facie case challenge to institution is reviewable; held unappealable under Cuozzo and 35 U.S.C. 314(d)
Under Cuozzo, this contention is not appealable.
4134: Jurisdiction over a non-final Veterans Court decision under the Williams v. Principi three-part test; the court found that the test was met and the Secretary could appeal.
This case satisfies the Williams test.
4150: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction to review decisions of a federal district court and its clerk on a default judgment request; held no jurisdiction under the Tucker Act.
Accordingly, the Claims Court correctly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction and properly dismissed Fuqua's complaint.
4158: Board jurisdiction over CDA appeals: the Board dismissed DAI's appeals for lack of jurisdiction based on the certification defect; the court held the Board has jurisdiction over the deemed-denied claims.
Because the Board has jurisdiction over DAI's appeals of its deemed denied claims, we reverse the Board's decision and remand for further proceedings.
4165: Mootness: Papst's appeals from the Board decisions in IPR2016-01839 and IPR2016-01864 were dismissed as moot because the affirmed claims included all claims held unpatentable in those proceedings, and the Board decisions were vacated.

Because those claims include all claims held unpatentable by the Board in IPR2016-01839 and IPR2016-01864, we dismiss as moot Papst's appeals from the decisions in IPR2016-08139 and IPR2016-01864 and vacate the decisions of the Board.
4173: Whether the Board has jurisdiction over Holland's termination appeal under the suitability regulations, 5 U.S.C. 7511/7513, 5 C.F.R. 315.805-.806, and the prohibited personnel practice allegations; the court held the Board lacks jurisdiction.
We agree that the Board lacks jurisdiction, and we therefore affirm, leaving the termination unreviewed.
4183: Appellate jurisdiction over a non-final Veterans Court remand order under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a) and the Williams exception; court held it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed.
We agree with the government that we lack jurisdiction.
4186: Jurisdiction over a mixed case: government argued the appeal became a mixed case; court held employee's Form 10 waiver of discrimination claims gave it jurisdiction
we will hold Ms. Harris to her formal waiver of any discrimination or retaliation claims decided by the MSPB, see Dkt. No. 13 (Form 10), and thus retain jurisdiction over this appeal
4188: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: whether the court can review the Veterans Court's determination that the claimant presented no new and material evidence and that the Board's error was harmless.

In conclusion, we do not have jurisdiction to review Mr. Bolden's appeal challenging the Veterans Court's judgment on the materiality of the evidence that he presented to reopen his claim for service connection for his chronic right ankle condition.
4207: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction to summon a grand jury or adjudicate criminal matters; the court held it lacks such jurisdiction.
Accordingly, the Court of Federal Claims did not abuse its discretion in concluding that it has no jurisdiction to summon a grand jury.
4211: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over Veterans Court appeal limited by 38 U.S.C. § 7292; court held it lacked jurisdiction because no legal error or constitutional issue was identified, only factual challenges.
We conclude that we do not have jurisdiction to review any of Mr. Haynes's arguments on appeal, though his arguments are less than clear.
4215: Mootness of Teva's cross-appeal from the injunction order: the court dismissed the cross-appeal as moot because the requested stay had already been granted under Rule 8.
Because we have already granted the relief requested in Teva's cross-appeal, see No. 19-2396, ECF No. 43, we dismiss Teva's cross-appeal as moot.
4216: Board lacked jurisdiction over retirement annuity computation claims after OPM rescinded its final reconsideration decision, so no final OPM decision conferred jurisdiction.
After OPM rescinded its October 31, 2017 final decision, there was no final OPM decision that would confer jurisdiction on the Board.
4217: Board lacked jurisdiction over involuntary retirement and negative suitability claims because an ODNI employee is excluded from the reach of 5 U.S.C. § 7511.

Ogburn, as an ODNI employee, is excluded from the reach of 5 U.S.C. § 7511, and the Board therefore lacked jurisdiction over Ogburn's claims of involuntary retirement action and negative suitability determination.
4218: Court of Appeals' jurisdiction over Veterans Court equitable tolling decision; court held no reviewable legal error under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction
We therefore dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2).
4236: Mootness and Article III jurisdiction: the 19 claims held patent-ineligible in Twitter were moot, so the Board's decisions on them were vacated and remanded for dismissal; the 15 nonoverlapping claims were not moot and the court kept jurisdiction over them.
We vacate-in-part the Board's final written decisions only as to these overlapping claims and direct the Board to dismiss Apple's petitions as to these claims.
4244: Mootness: appeal dismissed as moot because OPM granted the relief sought regarding the military service deposit, so no live controversy remains on that issue.
It appears that OPM has granted Saxiones the relief he seeks regarding the deposit, so there is no longer a live case or controversy on that issue before us.
4246: Board lacked jurisdiction to review OPM's nonfinal decision on FERS disability annuity termination; appeal dismissed as premature.
Because the Board correctly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction to review the Office of Personnel Management's ("OPM") nonfinal decision, we affirm.
4266: Whether the Veterans Court had power under the All Writs Act and 38 U.S.C. § 7252 to award money damages for an alleged breach of confidentiality or as settlement of benefits claims; court held it lacked that power.
We affirm the court's determination that it lacked the power to grant this relief.
4267: Lack of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over appeal challenges to VA benefits rulings not yet decided by the Veterans Court, and over application of the new-and-material-evidence standard to particular facts.
But we lack jurisdiction to address such claims, for at least the following reasons.
4285: Mootness of defendants' cross-appeal challenging validity of the Elan patent and the resulting injunction, which expired July 30, 2018; cross-appeal dismissed as moot
Because the injunction terminated by its terms on the date of expiration of the Elan patent (July 30, 2018), and no retrospective liability is at issue, the cross-appeal is dismissed as moot.
4286: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court held it lacked jurisdiction because the appeal raised only factual issues or application of law to fact, and dismissed.
Because we lack jurisdiction to review such issues, Cook v. Principi, 353 F.3d 937, 939 (Fed. Cir. 2003); see also 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), we dismiss.
4292: Jurisdiction of the Veterans Court to hear appeal where the Board decision was vacated before notice of appeal was filed; no final decision existed.

Because the Board decision that formed the basis for Petitioner's appeal was properly vacated before a notice of appeal was filed, however, the Veterans Court did not have jurisdiction to hear the appeal.
4297: Whether the Court of Federal Claims had subject-matter jurisdiction under the Tucker Act over a negligence/theft-of-domain-names complaint with no identified federal responsibility.
Based on the record before us, we hold that the CFC lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over Ms. Waller's complaint.
4304: Court of Federal Claims lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over claims based on actions of federal district judges in other litigation (due process and conspiracy allegations).
The Claims Court was correct in holding that it lacked jurisdiction to consider any of Mr. Jarvis's allegations.
4308: Appellate jurisdiction over appeal from noninfringement judgment based on claim construction (Jang challenge); court held jurisdiction exists
We conclude that we have jurisdiction over EnerPol's appeal.
4311: Whether the district court had subject matter jurisdiction over the 2014 suit on a patent that issued after the ANDA was filed but before the Paragraph IV certification
We agree with Vanda that the district court had jurisdiction over this case.
4319: Whether the Board could review the propriety of the classification of the information in the emails under Executive Order 13,526; the court held the Board lacks authority to assess national security determinations and declined to reach that argument.
We agree with the MSPB that the Board is not a proper forum for resolving such a dispute since the Board does not have authority to assess the propriety of national security determinations.
4327: Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) to review the Veterans Court's weighing of service-connection evidence, the application of the duty to assist, and the application of the benefit-of-the-doubt rule to the facts; appeal dismissed.
We therefore conclude that we lack jurisdiction to hear his appeal.
4329: Jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction over Langan's claims against non-federal defendants, constitutional claims, statutory claims (28 U.S.C. 1493, 1498, 42 U.S.C. 1983) and equitable relief; dismissal affirmed.
The Claims Court was correct to dismiss Mr. Langan's complaint for lack of jurisdiction.
4332: Whether Congress displaced Tucker Act jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over the NRCS cooperative agreement claim in favor of administrative exhaustion followed by district court review; court held the CFC lacked subject-matter jurisdiction.

we hold that Congress displaced Tucker Act jurisdiction over claims against the NRCS such as St. Bernard's and imposed in its place a regime requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies, followed by judicial review in a district court.
4344: Justiciability of the challenge to the SecAF's manpower-driven modification of DoDI 1320.08, which the government argued was nonjusticiable; court held procedural violations are generally justiciable.
Although claims that military decisions are substantively wrong are nonjusticiable, procedural violations underlying military decisions are generally justiciable.
4356: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court: court lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292 because appellant raised no legal or constitutional challenge, only a factual challenge and application of law to facts
Because we lack jurisdiction, we dismiss.
4362: Government argued the Veterans Court exceeded its jurisdiction by considering Lang's finality argument raised first on appeal to that court; the Federal Circuit held the Veterans Court properly exercised jurisdiction and that it may review the underlying legal issues.
And because the Veterans Court properly exercised jurisdiction over Lang's argument, we have authority to review any underlying legal issues on appeal.
4367: Appellate jurisdiction: because Bank lacked standing, the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the appeal and dismissed it.
Because Mr. Bank lacks standing, we do not have jurisdiction to review this appeal.
4369: Court vacated the Rule 12 dismissal and remanded so the district court could determine in the first instance whether Uniloc has standing and cure any jurisdictional defects arising from the ownership transfers; no jurisdictional finding was made on appeal.
we remand for the district court to supplement the record, determine whether Uniloc has standing in the first instance, and, if appropriate, cure any jurisdictional defects.
4373: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over Wine's individual right of action appeal, which turned on whether OSC's investigation or inaction was a covered personnel action under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(a)(2)(A)(xii); the court held no non-frivolous allegation of a personnel action, so no jurisdiction.
Because the Board did not err in finding that Mr. Wine failed to identify a qualifying personnel action that OSC had taken against him, we affirm the Board's dismissal of his appeal.
4376: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: review of the Veterans Court's mandamus denial is allowed, but the court lacks jurisdiction over factual determinations and the merits of the underlying compensation claims, which the appellant asked it to decide.
Accordingly, there is no reviewable Veterans Court decision with respect to the merits of those claims.
4432: Mootness: government argued Board remand mooted the case; court held case not moot and that it has jurisdiction over the legal standard question
In light of the above, it is clear that the Board's remand did not provide all of the relief Mrs. Mote requested, that a case or controversy remains, and that we may adjudicate it.
4434: Jurisdiction under the Indian Tucker Act over the failure-to-maintain-sufficient-security portion of Claim I, which the Court of Federal Claims had dismissed under 12(b)(1).

Accordingly, the portion of Claim I that arises from the Government's alleged breach of its fiduciary duty to "hold in trust the security" against Collier's payment obligations . . . states a claim over which the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction, and upon which relief can be granted.
4440: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over a Veterans Court appeal under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction because the appeal challenged factual determinations and application of law to fact, not a statute or regulation interpretation or a constitutional issue, and dismissed the appeal.
Because Mr. Lopez's arguments all center on the application of law to fact and do not present constitutional issues, the court lacks jurisdiction to hear this appeal.
