We find that the district court's denial of Puritan's partial motion to dismiss does not conclusively determine any issue. Therefore, Puritan has not shown that the collateral order doctrine's requirements are satisfied. Accordingly, we dismiss for lack of appellate jurisdiction.
12571: Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) because the appeal challenged the Veterans Court's application of law to fact (harmless-error determination) regarding the Board's mischaracterization of the NOD; appeal dismissed.
we determine we lack jurisdiction to consider the Veterans Court's decision.
12574: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 to review the Veterans Court's dismissal of the post-September 7, 2018 headache rating claim and its treatment of statutory and regulatory interpretation; held no jurisdiction.
In sum, we do not have jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's dismissal decision.
12604: Whether the AJ and Board had authority to adjudicate an alleged obstruction violation under 18 U.S.C. § 1505; held they lack authority over criminal statutes.
Neither the AJ nor the Board have authority to adjudicate alleged violations of a criminal statute
12617: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims: dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction over claims against non-federal defendants, challenges to Florida Supreme Court decisions, and claims against the US lacking a money-mandating source of law.
The Claims Court correctly concluded that Ms. Rodriguez's filings fail to establish jurisdiction.
12618: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction over an illegal exaction or taking claim that would require review of a federal district court's turnover order; held no jurisdiction to provide collateral review of another federal court's decisions.
The Court of Federal Claims has no jurisdiction to provide collateral review of another federal court's decisions.
12624: Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction over Boeing's CDA contract claims (Counts I-III), including the court's power to resolve the validity of FAR 30.606 as inextricably intertwined with a contract dispute.
we conclude that the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction under the CDA to resolve this contract dispute and the validity of the underlying regulation.
12625: Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1) over Boeing's alternative illegal exaction claim (Count IV), which the trial court had held it lacked authority to consider because the CDA applied.
Count IV was properly asserted under the Court of Federal Claims's § 1491(a)(1) jurisdiction, see Boeing, 968 F.3d at 1383, and should have been adjudicated accordingly.
12631: Board jurisdiction over involuntary retirement appeal: whether the employee's nonfrivolous allegations of a hostile work environment entitled her to a jurisdictional hearing, and whether the AJ erred by discounting allegations as remote and weighing evidence pre-hearing.
We hold that the Board erred in its pre-hearing jurisdictional analysis.
12633: Whether the court has authority to re-review the 1997 Postal Service removal decision, which was previously affirmed; the court held the theory was not properly before it.
As to Mr. Casimier's first theory, that question relates to an appeal that is not properly before us.
12645: 28 U.S.C. § 1500 deprived the Claims Court of jurisdiction over the surviving continuing-trespass portions of Counts One, Two, Five and Six because the earlier-filed Nevada district court action arose from substantially the same operative facts
we affirm the Claims Court's dismissal under section 1500.
12646: Claims Court lacked jurisdiction to grant the equitable relief (documents and accounting) sought in Count Eight because no monetary claims remained to which it could be ancillary
Because none of the Colony's claims for monetary relief remain pending, we affirm the Claims Court's dismissal of Count Eight.
12650: MSPB lacked jurisdiction over probationary removal because appellant was not an 'employee' under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1)(A); Board dismissal affirmed
Thus, Ms. Gholston was a probationary employee at the time of her termination and does not meet the definition of "employee" under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1)(A)(i).
12651: Appellate jurisdiction limited under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: appeal dismissed because the claimant's challenges were to factual findings, which the court cannot review.

Those assertions amount to challenges to the Veterans Court's factual findings. It is not within our jurisdiction to review whether the Veterans Court incorrectly found, from the facts of record, that Mr. Wilbanks's disabilities have no service connection.
12652: Board jurisdiction: the Board lacked jurisdiction to reopen Koke's 2002 removal appeal after he withdrew it, absent unusual circumstances such as misinformation or new and material evidence.
Mr. Koke does not argue that the Board and the administrative judge erred in determining that the Board lacks jurisdiction to reopen and hear his appeal challenging his removal.
12666: Reviewability of real-party-in-interest challenges under 35 U.S.C. §314(d) (jurisdiction to review institution-related RPI challenges under §312(a)(2)); court held unreviewable
we conclude that FedEx's real party in interest-related challenges are unreviewable under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d).
12670: Mootness and appellate jurisdiction over MSN's appeal of the no-invalidity (nonobviousness) judgment on claim 3 of the '349 patent; appeal dismissed as moot and the district court judgment vacated under Munsingwear because Exelixis dropped its cross-appeal.
Having determined that MSN's appeal as to claim 3 is moot, the appropriate resolution in this case is vacatur of the district court's judgment on this claim.
12675: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. §7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's untimeliness and equitable tolling determinations because the appeal raised only factual determinations and applications of law to facts, with no constitutional issue.
As Mr. Lemmon does not raise a constitutional issue and only challenges factual determinations or applications of law to the facts of this case, we lack jurisdiction to review his arguments.
12681: Board jurisdiction: the court held that a separate challenge to the non-promotion decision is not an appealable adverse action under 5 U.S.C. 7512 and gives no independent basis for Board jurisdiction.

To the extent that Mr. Winfield attempts to challenge the non-promotion decision separately from his whistleblower claims, that is not an appealable adverse action under 5 U.S.C. § 7512 that would provide Mr. Winfield with an independent basis for Board jurisdiction.
12690: Jurisdiction: Court lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 because appeal challenged a factual determination (whether veteran was notified he needed to submit additional form).
We lack jurisdiction over Mr. Solomon’s appeal, we dismiss.
12697: Veterans Court's jurisdiction over Gonzalez's CUE motion: the Veterans Court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the CUE motion was directed to an already-affirmed DIC eligibility determination, and the Federal Circuit found no error.

We see no error in the Veterans Court's conclusion that Mr. González's CUE motion is directed to the previously affirmed determination denying his DIC eligibility and that it therefore lacked jurisdiction.
12698: Mootness: the appeal from the Board's unpatentability decision was dismissed as moot because the companion appeal in Xerox v. Snap affirmed obviousness of all claims of the same patent.

Because we affirm the Board's decision holding all claims of the '439 patent unpatentable as obvious in Xerox Corporation v. Snap, Inc., No. 2023-1967 (Fed. Cir. April 17, 2025), we dismiss this appeal as moot.
12699: Personal jurisdiction over Formycon in the preliminary injunction proceeding; the court held the record supports jurisdiction in West Virginia.
Regarding personal jurisdiction, the record as a whole reliably shows Formycon's plan to market FYB203 in West Virginia, and in other States.
12706: Jurisdiction to review a nonfinal Veterans Court remand order under the Williams conditions; the court held the third Williams requirement unmet and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Dodson's arguments do not change the fact that the Veterans Court issued a non-final order which we have no jurisdiction to review.
12712: Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction under the Tucker Act; complaint dismissed sua sponte for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because no substantive source of law mandating compensation was identified
For this reason, Mr. Khuc failed to show that the Court of Federal Claims was authorized to hear his case.
12716: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court denial of mandamus petition; court held it lacks jurisdiction because the petition did not present a non-frivolous legal question.
Accordingly, we conclude that we lack jurisdiction over this appeal and are required to dismiss it.
12729: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the application of law to fact in the CUE determination.

To the extent that Mr. Combs challenges the Veterans Court's determination that he did not clearly and unmistakeably establish that his symptoms approximated the 60% rating, that is an application of law to fact over which we lack jurisdiction.
12735: Appellate jurisdiction over an appeal from the denial of a motion to dismiss or transfer venue; the court held there was no final decision, no certified §1292(b) order, and no collateral-order or mandamus basis.
Because the decision of the district court is neither a final judgment nor otherwise properly before us, we dismiss.
12749: Board lacked jurisdiction over the IRA challenges to the 2018-2021 personnel actions because the appellant failed to make a nonfrivolous allegation that his protected disclosures contributed to those actions.
the remaining portion of Mr. Abresch's IRA case is properly dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
12756: Personal jurisdiction over Celltrion in West Virginia, challenged on appeal and resolved by SB Opinion conceded by Celltrion
we conclude, "based on the record and findings presented to us, that [Celltrion's] conduct satisfies the minimum-contacts requirement for personal jurisdiction in West Virginia,"
12761: Federal Circuit subject-matter jurisdiction over the appeals, which the court analyzed and found lacking because appellants lacked standing; court did not reach mootness.
Therefore, the parties have no remaining case or controversy and we lack jurisdiction. Thus, we dismiss both appeals.
12777: Scope of the court's jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court may review the statutory interpretation the Veterans Court did not address, but lacks jurisdiction to resolve the factual dispute over whether the claimant received the past-due payment before April 26, 2019.
Regardless of whether this argument was properly raised, we lack jurisdiction to resolve such factual disputes under these circumstances.
12790: Appellate jurisdiction over the Veterans Court decision: the court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the appellant raised only factual challenges and applications of law to fact barred by 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), and a constitutional label did not confer jurisdiction.
We therefore dismiss this appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
12804: Commission's authority under Section 337 to reach infringement based on post-importation user features and inducement, following Suprema
We are bound by this precedent and, accordingly, reject Google's argument.
12822: Jurisdiction: whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 over the claimant's challenge to the Board's effective-date determination for TDIU, which the court held presented only factual determinations and application of law to fact.
Because we lack jurisdiction to review factual determinations or the application of law to fact, we must dismiss.
12824: Court declined AML's request to vacate the ineligibility dismissal or declare it nonpreclusive, treating that request as an advisory opinion outside Article III jurisdiction.
We reject AML's request for what is essentially an advisory opinion on the preclusive effect that the district court's judgment (and ours) might have in future cases.
12837: Board jurisdiction over involuntary retirement (constructive removal) claim; court held no nonfrivolous allegation of involuntariness, so no jurisdiction.
We agree with the Board that Ms. Johnson has failed to make non-frivolous allegations that her retirement was involuntary, such that it would constitute a constructive removal.
12840: Board's jurisdiction over the IRA appeal: whether the appellant nonfrivolously alleged protected disclosures that were contributing factors in the personnel action; Board dismissal for lack of jurisdiction affirmed.
Because the Board properly determined that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Coleman's appeal, we affirm.
12849: Jurisdiction to review challenges to the validity of 38 C.F.R. 3.700 and the applicability of a VA general counsel opinion; court lacked jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292(c) because the Veterans Court did not rely on or address these arguments.
Accordingly, we do not have jurisdiction to review these challenges.
12850: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over veteran's appeal: CUE claim not raised before the Veterans Court and as-applied challenge to 38 C.F.R. 3.1(p) and 3.155(a) barred by 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2); appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
We lack jurisdiction over his appeal and, accordingly, dismiss.
12851: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over a Veterans Court decision under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the appeal was dismissed because the veteran raised no legal challenge, only factual determinations and as-applied challenges, which § 7292(d)(2) bars.
Mr. Sylvain does not raise any challenge over which we can exercise jurisdiction, as he does not allege any legal error by the Veterans Court.
12855: Mootness: MSPB dismissal of indefinite suspension appeal as moot because the agency rescinded the suspension and paid back pay
the MSPB did not err in its dismissal of the administrative appeal as moot.
12862: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292(a): the parties disputed whether the court had jurisdiction, and the court held it had jurisdiction because the veteran raised a statutory-interpretation question relied upon by the Veterans Court.
Mr. Trulson raised such an issue regarding § 1114(r) before the Veterans Court.
12864: Lack of jurisdiction over arguments not raised before the Veterans Court (earlier effective date under 38 U.S.C. 5110 and equitable tolling; caregiver stipend under PCAFC).
We lack jurisdiction over issues not raised before the Veterans Court.
12865: Board jurisdiction over IRA appeal: court held Board did not err in finding administrative exhaustion limited to the grievance, and that the grievance-based protected activity did not establish jurisdiction under the 2302(b)(9) limit.
the Board did not err in finding that she had only exhausted her OSC remedies with respect to her claim that the IRS retaliated against her for filing the March 2, 2023 grievance.
12868: Lack of Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction because no money-mandating statute was identified and the Airman's Medal award is a nonjusticiable discretionary military judgment.
Mr. Avery fails to provide a money-mandating statute to invoke the Claims Court's jurisdiction
12873: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: Secretary argued the appeal merely challenged application of law to facts; court held it lacked jurisdiction over the issue-exhaustion challenge and the application of 38 C.F.R. § 3.400 to the facts, and dismissed the appeal.
Accordingly, we lack jurisdiction over Mr. Belger’s appeal.
12890: Mootness: the case is not moot as to the class claims under the inherently transitory exception, so the Veterans Court's mootness dismissal is vacated.
We agree with appellants and conclude that these requirements are met in this case; therefore, it is not moot.
12891: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacks jurisdiction because the appeal challenges the application of Roberson to the facts (application of law to fact), not a legal question.
We lack jurisdiction over Ms. Campbell's appeal because the Board and Veterans Court applied Roberson.
12893: Jurisdiction and mootness: the court held the abandonment challenge moot after revival and lacked jurisdiction over the patent term adjustment request because no patent issued and such challenges belong in the Eastern District of Virginia.
We lack jurisdiction over the abandonment and patent term adjustment issues.
12895: Reviewability under the APA: the Commission's refusal to enter a show cause order sua sponte is committed to agency discretion under 5 U.S.C. § 701(a)(2), so the appeal is unreviewable and dismissed. The court did not reach standing or statutory jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(6) and 19 U.S.C. § 1337(c).
We conclude that the Commission's refusal to enter a show cause order sua sponte is within the agency's discretion and therefore unreviewable.
12896: Reviewability under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d): Zillow argued the scope-of-petition challenge was barred as closely tied to institution; the court held § 314(d) does not bar review.
Section 314(d) accordingly does not bar us from reviewing IBM's challenge.
12905: Reviewability of the Board's §311(b) ruling under 35 U.S.C. §314(d) (Apple argued the challenge was an unreviewable institution decision); court held the appeal reviewable.
We conclude that Qualcomm's appeal is reviewable.
12911: Board jurisdiction over the IRA appeal: the court held the Board properly dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because Hawker did not nonfrivolously allege a protected disclosure that was a contributing factor in a personnel action.
To establish Board jurisdiction over individual right of action cases, the appellant must make 'non-frivolous allegations' that he engaged in whistleblowing activity by making a protected disclosure
12926: Jurisdiction/mootness in the changed-circumstances review case: court rejected the Trade Court's mootness ground and held the case was not moot.
Therefore, the case was and is not moot.
12928: Subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §1581(i) over challenge to the Commission's denial of reconsideration: court held the Trade Court lacked §1581(i) jurisdiction because §1581(c) was available and not manifestly inadequate.
Consequently, the Trade Court lacked § 1581(i) subject-matter jurisdiction.
12938: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court lacked jurisdiction to review the application of law to fact in the knee rating (diagnostic codes), constitutional labels that did not confer jurisdiction, and arguments not raised before the Veterans Court (CUE, 1982 denial, 1968/1970 injury records).
Because Mr. Shannon's appeal does not present issues within our limited jurisdiction, we dismiss.
12948: Jurisdiction over the NOD and JMPR content argument: the court lacks jurisdiction because interpreting the contents of the 2020 NOD and the JMPR is a factual question beyond its review under 38 U.S.C. 7292, so the argument is dismissed.
Because we lack jurisdiction over this issue, we must dismiss it.
12949: Whether the Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction because the Board never made an adverse decision on effective dates for the new SMC(o) and (r) awards; the court affirmed that no adverse Board decision triggered jurisdiction.
The Veterans Court did not err in holding the same.
12953: Jurisdiction of the Veterans Court: whether the Board's March 2024 remand-type order was a reviewable final Board decision under 38 U.S.C. § 7252, so that the Veterans Court had jurisdiction; the Secretary moved to dismiss and the court held there was no reviewable decision.
We therefore agree with the Veterans Court that there was no final Board decision and that dismissal for lack of jurisdiction was appropriate.
12968: Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction over a CUE claim against the September 1982 rating decision because the theory was never presented to the RO or decided by the Board; the Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal.
Because that claim was not addressed on the merits by the Board or the Veterans Court, it likewise is not reviewable by this court.
12969: Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction over the challenge to the Veterans Court's application of settled law to the facts in the CUE claim against the December 1991 RO rating decision, and dismissed it.
Because we are not permitted to review this direct application of law to the factual circumstances of this case, we dismiss this claim for lack of jurisdiction.
12972: Subject-matter jurisdiction under the Declaratory Judgment Act: no case or controversy between USAA and Mitek as to direct, induced, or contributory infringement, so the district court lacked jurisdiction over the non-infringement claims.

we agree with the district court's determination that the record evidence, including USAA's allegations, arguments, and claim charts from the Wells Fargo Case, which cited to Mitek documentation as evidence of infringement for only some of many claim limitations, did not give rise to a case or controversy between USAA and Mitek as to direct, induced, or contributory infringement.
12981: Jurisdiction: the district court lacked jurisdiction over the general damages and Takings Clause claims because they exceed $10,000 and belong in the Court of Federal Claims; no waiver of sovereign immunity for money damages under §§ 1331, 1338 or § 145.
thus, the district court did not err in finding it lacked jurisdiction over her general damages claim and damages under the Takings Clause claim.
12997: Tucker Act jurisdiction: the court held the RRF statute, 15 U.S.C. § 9009c, is money-mandating, so the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction. The Government contested this under Katz, Bowen, Lummi and National Center.
we hold the RRF statute is money-mandating.
13002: Lack of jurisdiction over discrimination claim under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2)
we do not have jurisdiction to address a claim for discrimination under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2).
13003: Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) to review factual determinations and application of law to fact in the veteran's appeal; appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Those arguments involve challenges to factual determinations or application of law to fact, which we lack jurisdiction to consider.
13013: Board jurisdiction over IRA appeal: lack of OSC exhaustion for two disclosures (traffic citation abuse and retaliation), so the Board lacked jurisdiction over those claims

The Board correctly concluded that Mr. Tarrab failed to allege administrative exhaustion regarding two of his alleged disclosures and that it thus lacked jurisdiction over any claim regarding these disclosures.
13018: Jurisdictional limits under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: Court lacked jurisdiction to review challenges to the Board's weighing of evidence and adequacy of reasons, duty-to-assist compliance, and claim-scope interpretation, all factual matters, and a constitutional-characterization argument that did not present a constitutional issue.
We lack jurisdiction to review Mr. Bradley's first three alleged errors, which amount to factual disagreements with the outcome of his case.
13025: Mootness of the appeal as to the '325 patent. Because all claims were invalidated in prior district court litigation, the court held the appeal moot and dismissed it for lack of a live controversy.
Therefore, with respect to the ’325 patent, we dismiss the appeal as moot.
13039: Mootness after petitioners' settlement and withdrawal from the appeal; the court analyzed whether a live controversy remained and found one, so it reached the merits.
Despite this withdrawal, a live controversy regarding the patentability of Netlist's claims remains before us for resolution.
13040: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over §1983 claims, tort claims, and the asserted implied-in-fact contract with the PTO (Tucker Act). The court held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction and dismissed.
We agree with the Court of Federal Claims that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction and, accordingly, affirm its dismissal of Dr. Pulnikova's complaint.
13041: Whether mandamus relief under the All Writs Act was available to compel VA to continue benefits pending appeal, given the adequate alternative remedy by appeal; court held the Veterans Court properly dismissed the mandamus petitions for lack of jurisdiction.
Because there was an alternative remedy by appeal, the Veterans Court did not err in dismissing the petitions for writs of mandamus.
13045: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: whether Perry's appeal raised a legal or constitutional challenge within the court's narrow review of Veterans Court orders denying extraordinary relief; the court held it did not and dismissed.
As such, Mr. Perry fails to raise a challenge to the Veterans Court's June 2024 order that falls within our narrow appellate jurisdiction.
13064: Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process claims.
this Court has made clear that the Claims Court does not have jurisdiction to consider claims arising under the Due Process clauses of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.
13067: Jurisdiction over challenge to Board's factual determination that no formal or informal IBS claim was filed before April 24, 2006; court lacks jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2).

This is a challenge to the Board's factual determination that Mr. Roberts "had not filed formal or informal claims for [IBS] prior to [April 24, 2006]." We therefore lack jurisdiction over this claim.
13081: Board dismissed employee's appeal for lack of jurisdiction because OPM rescinded its reconsideration decision, divesting the Board of jurisdiction; Federal Circuit affirmed on the merits.
We therefore affirm, on the merits, the Board's dismissal of Mr. Sanders's appeal in the I-1 case.
13085: Board jurisdiction: whether Jones was an 'employee' under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1)(B) (similar positions), so the Board had jurisdiction over his constructive-discharge appeal; the Board lacked jurisdiction.
We thus affirm the Board's ultimate determination that it lacked jurisdiction to hear Jones's appeal.
13086: Jurisdiction over Counts 1 and 2: annuity calculation claims fall within OPM's exclusive authority and MSPB review under 5 U.S.C. 8461, so the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction.
The Claims Court correctly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction over Counts 1 and 2.
13087: Jurisdiction over Count 3: health premium refund claim not supported by a money-mandating source of law, so no Tucker Act jurisdiction.
The Claims Court correctly determined that it lacked jurisdiction over Count 3.
13088: Jurisdiction over Count 4: FECA claim, where Congress vested decisions in the Secretary of Labor and foreclosed judicial review, so FECA cannot supply jurisdiction.
Therefore, this statute cannot provide a basis for the Claims Court's jurisdiction, and the Claims Court properly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction over Count 4.
13090: Jurisdiction over purely injunctive relief for breach of the Labor settlement agreement: the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over injunctive relief not incident of or collateral to a money judgment.
the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over a claim for injunctive relief that is not "incident of or collateral to" a money judgment.
13092: Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over constitutional claims (Fourth, Sixth, Fourteenth Amendments) because they are not money-mandating.
We have repeatedly held that the constitutional claims asserted by Mr. Horn are not money-mandating.
13094: Whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over an appeal of a reduction in on-call premium pay; the court held on-call pay is not basic pay, so the reduction is not an appealable reduction in pay and the MSPB lacked jurisdiction.
Thus, a reduction in on-call pay does not count as a "reduction in pay" under § 7511(a)(4) because on-call pay is not basic pay.
13096: Pendent appellate jurisdiction over non-appealable Markman and summary judgment orders, disputed by the parties; court found jurisdiction.
We agree with Schmeisser that the doctrine of pendent appellate jurisdiction applies in this instance.
13098: Board jurisdiction over IRA appeal: whether the Board had jurisdiction because the denied leave-classification requests were personnel actions not barred by Egan security-clearance review

Accordingly, because Akerman's IRA appeal did not make a non-frivolous allegation that NGB took an adverse personnel action against him, the Board correctly held that it did not have jurisdiction over his appeal.
13106: Appellate jurisdiction over a non-final Veterans Court remand order; the Williams exception to finality was not satisfied, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because this non-final order does not fall into the limited class of orders that we will consider under Williams v. Principi, 275 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2002), we dismiss.
13107: Limits under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court lacks jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's factual determinations (abandonment of the 70 percent PTSD rating claim and the 2018 effective-date determination) and application of law to fact.
As discussed previously, however, we lack jurisdiction to review factual determinations or the application of law to fact in appeals from the Veterans Court absent a constitutional issue.
13119: Jurisdiction: the court analyzed the limits on its review of OPM disability determinations under 5 U.S.C. § 8347 and Lindahl, holding that legal issues are reviewable and that it may address the Board's legal error.
Issues of law, however, are reviewable. Id. Thus, we may address Ms. Garland's argument that the Board made a critical legal error in reviewing OPM's decision.
13120: Jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims: Fifth and Thirteenth Amendment claims are not money-mandating, and tort and human-trafficking claims are outside Tucker Act jurisdiction; dismissal for lack of jurisdiction affirmed.
"[t]he Thirteenth Amendment is not a money-mandating authority that provides jurisdiction."
13121: Jurisdiction over claims arising under the 1836 Treaty of Peace and Friendship with Morocco: treaty claims with foreign nations are excluded from Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1502; treaty is not an Act of Congress.
"[c]laims arising under treaties with foreign nations are expressly excluded from the jurisdiction" of the Court of Federal Claims.
13133: Limits on review under 38 U.S.C. 502: court declined to review fact-specific, as-applied challenges to agency action in the Lathams' own case.
To the extent the Lathams are questioning specific agency action taken in relation to their specific situation, we are not permitted to review such disputes under 38 U.S.C. § 502.
13144: Threshold mootness argument by Spectrum rejected; court held the claim construction appeal is not moot.
Accordingly, the district court's claim construction is not moot.
13160: Whether the court can review the agency's compliance with the MSPB final order and interim relief, where no enforcement petition was filed with the MSPB
Any issues Mr. Martinez has concerning the agency's compliance with the MSPB's final order are therefore not properly before this court.
13161: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court dismissed because Jones's challenges were factual or applied law to facts, and her constitutional, CUE, EAJA and Rule 55 arguments did not present reviewable questions.
Because Ms. Jones' challenges are all factual in nature, we do not have jurisdiction.
13170: Board jurisdiction over May's Title VII discrimination arguments in an IRA appeal and the request to treat the case as a mixed case: the Board lacks jurisdiction over discrimination claims in a WPA case.
The Board has no jurisdiction to address May's arguments concerning Title VII discrimination as part of the WPA case
13172: Board jurisdiction over an involuntary retirement appeal by a DEA SES employee: whether 5 U.S.C. 3151(a)(5)(D) removes Board appeal rights, so the Board lacked jurisdiction.
We conclude that the Board correctly construed the relevant statute and that the Board lacked jurisdiction.
13199: Mootness of Counts I-III and V after the Navy's corrective action rescinded the January 4, 2024 SeaPort-NxG modification; the court held no live case remained, so the CFC lacked jurisdiction over these counts.
For these reasons, the Navy's Corrective Action mooted I–III and V and we affirm the Federal Claims Court's dismissal of these counts.
13200: FASA task order bar (10 U.S.C. § 3406(f)) under which Count IV, a bid protest in connection with the issuance of task orders, is outside the CFC's bid protest jurisdiction.
For these reasons, FASA bars Count IV of Island Creek's complaint.
13205: Scope of appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1295(a)(9): the court held it could review only the final Board decision, so it did not reach the merits-based due process argument about an oral reply.
we may only review final decisions of the Board, 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), and the final decision here does not address the merits of Ms. Kulowiec's appeal
13213: Jurisdiction: whether the Veterans Court properly dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction and the limits on Federal Circuit review under 38 U.S.C. 7292 (review of application of law to fact and factual determinations barred); court held it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed.
Because we lack jurisdiction over Mr. Onofre's appeal, we dismiss.
13215: Board jurisdiction: whether the MSPB has jurisdiction over an appeal of a proposed removal, which is not an appealable adverse action under 5 U.S.C. § 7512. Court held the Board lacks jurisdiction and affirmed.
Because mere proposals to remove are not listed in § 7512, they are not appealable adverse actions in themselves and the Board has no jurisdiction over them.
13240: Justiciability of challenge to Air Force Board for Correction of Military Records denial of retirement grade relief; court held claim justiciable at least in part under Fisher and Bader
We conclude that Mr. Gersten's claims are justiciable at least in part under Fisher and Bader.
13254: Jurisdiction: the court lacked jurisdiction over the appeal of the MSPB's denial of reopening because the termination appeal was a mixed case subject to the mixed-case jurisdictional bar (5 U.S.C. 7702, 7703(b)).
We therefore conclude that we lack jurisdiction.
13287: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d): the court held it lacked jurisdiction because the appeal challenges only the application of the TDIU regulation (38 C.F.R. § 4.16(a)) to the facts, and dismissed.
We conclude that we do not have jurisdiction over the instant appeal because Crider challenges only the application of the TDIU regulation, 38 C.F.R. § 4.16(a), to the facts of his case.
13288: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: whether the appeal presents a legal question reviewable by the court, as opposed to a pure application of law to fact or an as-applied challenge, and whether constitutional labels confer jurisdiction.
For that reason, this appeal does not fall within our jurisdiction to review decisions of the Veterans Court. The appeal therefore must be dismissed.
13295: Cross-appeal on punitive damages dismissed as moot because the underlying liability judgment was reversed.
we reverse the award of damages to Atturo and dismiss as moot Atturo's cross-appeal as to punitive damages.
13296: Mootness: the Board lacked jurisdiction after the agency rescinded the February 16, 2024 removal and returned the employee to status quo ante; the court found substantial evidence supported complete rescission and affirmed dismissal as moot.

Accordingly, we conclude that substantial evidence in the record supports the Board's finding regarding status quo ante relief; and therefore, the Board did not err in dismissing Mr. Thorogood's administrative appeal as moot.
13299: Jurisdiction over appeal of Veterans Court remand order on TBI effective date; remand for further explanation is not a reviewable final decision under the Williams v. Principi finality exception.
None of these conditions is satisfied here. The Veterans Court remanded for further explanation of the Board's decision so that the court could discharge its duty on appellate review.
13300: Jurisdiction over appeal of Veterans Court dismissal of 100% disability effective-date claim, which the Board never decided, under 38 U.S.C. 7252(a).
Mr. Hooper alleges no plausible error as to the Veterans Court's determination that it lacked jurisdiction over this issue, and we therefore lack jurisdiction over his appeal.
13301: Jurisdiction over appeal of Veterans Court dismissal of dental disability claim because the Board's remand was not a decision under 38 U.S.C. 7252(a).
Because the remand order contains no order granting or denying relief, it is not a decision within the meaning of section 7252(a).
13315: Tucker Act jurisdiction: Claims Court lacked jurisdiction because Wolf Creek was not in privity with the Army and American Ordnance was not the Army's agent; the Federal Circuit affirmed the jurisdictional dismissal.
We therefore affirm the Claims Court’s ruling that it lacked jurisdiction in this case and its dismissal of Wolf Creek’s case.
13319: Scope of the Board's jurisdiction in the IRA appeal: personnel actions and issues not first raised with OSC were properly excluded, and the Board's review does not extend to the merits of the agency's charge.
the Board's jurisdiction in an IRA appeal is "limited to those issues that have been previously raised with OSC."
13320: Subject matter jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims dismissed takings claim as time-barred under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for lack of jurisdiction; appellate court affirmed.
We affirm the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
13322: Law-of-the-case: whether the 2023 court could revisit the 2013 jurisdictional ruling sua sponte; court held no abuse of discretion.
The 2023 court did not abuse its discretion in revisiting the issue of subject matter jurisdiction.
13338: Mootness: appeal of the district court's summary judgment of patent invalidity dismissed as moot after the jury's unenforceability-based tying finding
Accordingly, Ingevity's appeal of the invalidity ruling is dismissed as moot.
13343: Jurisdiction/mootness: Kyocera's covenant not to sue extinguished any case or controversy, so the court lacked jurisdiction over the appeal.

13345: Court analyzed whether it had jurisdiction over the appeal as a possible mixed case involving discrimination, and held the appeal does not present a mixed case, so review proceeds in this court.
Thus, Mr. Akerman's appeal does not present a mixed case.
13348: Board's jurisdiction over habeas corpus and writ of replevin claims: no law, rule or regulation gives the Board jurisdiction, so dismissal was proper.
As such, the Board properly dismissed these claims.
13353: Mootness: appeal dismissed as moot as to claims previously held unpatentable by the Board and affirmed on appeal.
Therefore, with respect to these claims, we dismiss Express Mobile's appeal as moot.
13358: Limits on Federal Circuit review under 38 U.S.C. 7292: court lacked jurisdiction over challenge to VA factual determination and over constitutional due process claim found frivolous
Because we lack jurisdiction to hear portions of this appeal, we dismiss-in-part.
13368: Tucker Act jurisdiction: the Claims Court held that VJRA exclusivity (38 U.S.C. 511) barred jurisdiction over the breach claim because it concerns VA benefits; the Federal Circuit affirmed.

The review bar applies here because Mr. El Malik's claim would require review of 'questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the Secretary under a law that affects the provision of benefits by the Secretary to veterans.'
13372: Jurisdiction of the Veterans Court to review an RO decision absent a Board decision; whether the Veterans Court had jurisdiction over the October 2022 Board decision and the purported January 10, 2023 Board decision

13373: Board jurisdiction: the court held the Board lacked jurisdiction over the removal appeal because the employee, an excepted-service intelligence specialist, had no appeal rights under 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(8), and so the Board could not reach alleged agency wrongdoing.
Because Ms. Bombeva does not have Board appeal rights, the Board properly concluded that it did not have jurisdiction to address her allegations of agency wrongdoing.
13380: Whether the Board has jurisdiction to conduct IPR and cancel claims of an expired patent; court held the Board has jurisdiction.
confirmed that "the Board has jurisdiction over IPRs concerning expired patents."
13381: Jurisdiction over the Board's CAS 418 claim decision: the Board's quantum-remanded liability ruling was not a final decision, so the court dismissed that part of the appeal.
Therefore, we do not have jurisdiction over the CAS 418 Claim.
13382: Jurisdiction over the Board's Drag Claim decision: the Drag Claim was separate and final, so the court exercised jurisdiction over it.
Because the Board's decision as to the Drag Claim was separate and final, not requiring a further calculation, it was appealable, and we have jurisdiction over the Board's decision on the Drag Claim.
13396: Appellate jurisdiction: Seagate's cross-appeal on invalidity was improper because Seagate prevailed and raised invalidity only as an affirmative defense, so the cross-appeal was dismissed.
13402: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over an adverse action appeal of an alleged involuntary retirement by a title 38 VA registered nurse; the court held the nurse could not appeal as an adverse action because she was excluded from the competitive service under title 38.
Therefore, the Board did not err in finding that it lacked jurisdiction over Ms. Muhleisen's adverse action appeal.
13410: Scope of the court's jurisdiction under 5 U.S.C. § 8461(d) to review factual findings and weight given to mental diagnoses and outside disability awards in FERS disability cases.
we lack jurisdiction to do so.
13416: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court lacks jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's factual determinations and application of law to facts on the earlier effective date, and the remaining notice, due-process, and procedural arguments raise no issue within its limited review.

We lack jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's factual determinations or application of law to facts. We therefore dismiss Ms. Hayes-Libby's appeal regarding earlier effective date for her service-connection claims.
13423: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's affirmance of the Board's denial of a CUE motion, where the appeal challenges factual weighing of medical evidence and the alleged legal error was not the basis of the affirmance. Court held no jurisdiction and dismissed.
Because this court lacks jurisdiction, we must dismiss.
13435: Ripeness as a basis for dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under RCFC 12(b)(1): the regulatory takings claim was not ripe because United had not been denied an ESA Section 10 incidental-take permit.

Having yet to have been denied an incidental-take permit under Section 10 of the ESA, United has therefore not pleaded a ripe takings claim, and the district court properly dismissed its complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
13438: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over veterans appeal limited by 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2); court lacked jurisdiction to review application of §5110 to the facts and factual challenges
We lack jurisdiction to hear this appeal.
13462: Jurisdiction over salary claims: the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction to grant the equitable and prospective relief plaintiffs seek, and the court did not reach the constitutionality of the statutes.
In view of the foregoing, we conclude that the Federal Claims Court lacks jurisdiction to grant the relief that Plaintiffs request.
13463: Jurisdiction over retirement benefits claim challenging OPM's exclusion of COLA from retirement calculations: neither this court nor the Court of Federal Claims has jurisdiction because CSRS/FERS claims must go through OPM and the MSPB first.
We hold that neither this court nor the Federal Claims Court has jurisdiction to decide Plaintiffs' second retirement benefits claim.
13471: Jurisdiction: Mr. Ramey's notice of appeal failed to specify him as an appellant under FRAP 3(c), so the court lacks jurisdiction over the sanctions portion of the appeal
we dismiss this portion of the appeal for lack of jurisdiction and do not reach whether the district court abused its discretion in sanctioning Mr. Ramey.
13480: Appellate jurisdiction challenged by SCJ after ZT assigned the patent during the appeal; court held jurisdiction attached when the notice of appeal was filed and the assignment did not defeat it.
But our jurisdiction attached when the notice of appeal was filed.
13484: Court of Federal Claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction: claims against non-United States defendants, the §1983 civil rights claim, the state-law defamation tort claim, and criminal and constitutional claims lack a money-mandating source under the Tucker Act.
Because Mr. Dibrell's claims are outside the jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims, we affirm.
13491: Appellate jurisdiction: court lacked jurisdiction because the notice of appeal was untimely and the appeal must be dismissed
Thus, we lack jurisdiction over her claims and must dismiss.
13501: Board's jurisdiction over ex parte reexamination of an expired patent
We reject Gesture's argument here with respect to ex parte reexaminations and confirm that the Board has jurisdiction over ex parte reexaminations concerning expired patents.
13541: Jurisdiction over appeal of application of Rice v. Shinseki TDIU implicit-claim standard to facts; court lacks jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) as-applied bar
We lack jurisdiction over this issue because it involves the application of the legal standard stated in Rice to the facts of this case.
13548: Mootness: the cross-appeal from the denial of BPI's Rule 59 motion and the appeal from denial of the Rule 60(b) motion were dismissed as moot after reversal of the judgment.
In light of our reversal of the judgment, Appellants’ appeal of the denial of its Rule 60(b) motion and BPI’s cross-appeal are moot.
13552: Mootness: the appeal from the CIT's denial of the joint motion for confidential treatment was held moot because the information was released over two years earlier, and the capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception did not apply given the companion case decided the same day.
Under these circumstances, we agree with the Tenth Circuit that the issues presented in this appeal are moot and do not evade review.
13563: Subject matter jurisdiction: the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal under RCFC 12(b)(1) for lack of jurisdiction, based on the limitations-period jurisdictional facts, was affirmed.
We thus affirm the trial court's dismissal of Plaintiffs' amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
13586: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act subject matter jurisdiction over claims against private employers (LabCorp, Quest Diagnostics), including claims that they were federal contractors; the court analyzed this question on the merits.
The Claims Court properly found that it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over Ms. Beauvais's complaint.
13595: Board jurisdiction: whether the MSPB had appellate jurisdiction over Suggs's appeal of the denial of severance pay and the garnishment of his benefits, where wage garnishment is not an appealable adverse action under 5 U.S.C. § 7512 and no removal challenge was properly before the Board.

We agree. The Roach decision held that wage garnishment could satisfy the statutory definition of "personnel action" under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(a)(2)(A), allowing such action to support Board jurisdiction in an Individual Right of Action claim for whistleblower reprisal.
13604: Mootness of K2's appeal from denial of intervention; court held the appeal not moot because vacating the misrepresentation finding could benefit K2's pending termination-for-convenience suit.
That is enough to prevent mootness.
13607: Jurisdiction over the TBI effective-date claim: no final Board decision on the TBI claim, so the court lacked jurisdiction over it, including the due process notice argument
we do not have jurisdiction to hear his appeal with respect to his TBI benefits.
13608: Limits under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(2): challenges to application of law to fact (Shea/3.155 encompassing claim, CUE application, factual effective-date findings) are outside jurisdiction
We lack jurisdiction to review this application of law to fact.
13609: No jurisdiction over the 38 U.S.C. 5104A medical-judgment challenge because it was not raised before the Veterans Court
Mr. Hooper did not raise any such challenge before the Veterans Court, so we lack jurisdiction to review it.
13628: Board's jurisdiction over appeal of termination of AAFES nonappropriated fund instrumentality employee; Board lacked jurisdiction because NAFI employees are not employees under 5 U.S.C. 2105(c) for chapter 75 adverse action appeals and WPA purposes
we conclude that the Board did not err in holding that it lacked jurisdiction over Crandall's appeal.
13629: Appellate jurisdiction over an appeal from the Veterans Court's denial of a mandamus petition seeking an order compelling adjudication of veterans' claims; the court held the appeal raised only a factual challenge and that the constitutional reference was constitutional in name only, so it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed.
Under that principle, this case falls outside our jurisdiction.
13634: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: government argued no jurisdiction; court held the challenge to the Veterans Court's interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b) is a legal question within its review.

We disagree. We understand Mr. Brown to argue that the Veterans Court misinterpreted 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b) in ruling that the Board was not obligated to address whether the 1992 examination was new and material evidence
13636: Limits on review under § 7292(d)(2): Veterans Court's determinations about the 1998 and 2009 Board decisions are factual findings or application of law to fact and cannot be reviewed by the Federal Circuit.
The Veterans Court's determination, on appeal to us, is either a factual finding or an application of law to fact—neither of which we can review under our jurisdictional statute.
13638: Jurisdiction/ripeness: whether ripeness is a jurisdictional requirement; court declined to decide because the claim is unripe regardless
Resolution of this appeal does not require delving into these potential complexities
13642: Mootness of SCI's challenge to Commerce's suspension-of-liquidation instructions; court declined to reach forfeiture or merits because the challenge was moot.
We need not reach the issue of forfeiture or the merits because SCI's suspension of liquidation challenge is moot.
13645: Whether petitioner has a statutory right to seek judicial review of the MSPB final decision under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(a)(1); court lacks jurisdiction and dismisses
Because Mr. Dowling lacks a statutory right to seek judicial review under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(a)(1), we dismiss.
13648: Court of Federal Claims lacked subject matter jurisdiction over claims against individual federal judges and prosecutors, over claims barred by a pending district court suit under 28 U.S.C. § 1500, and over claims lacking a money-mandating source of law; equitable and trustee theories cannot expand jurisdiction.
Thus, the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over Miles' claims against the individual defendants named and properly dismissed those claims.
13653: Whether the Court of Federal Claims had jurisdiction over a claim to enforce an arbitration award against Toyota, a private party, rather than a Tucker Act money claim against the United States.

The Court of Federal Claims properly concluded that it did not have jurisdiction over Mr. Malone's claim, which is a request for enforcement of an alleged arbitration agreement against Toyota, not a claim for money damages against the United States under the Tucker Act.
13654: Federal Circuit jurisdiction limited under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): no jurisdiction over challenges to factual determinations or to application of law to facts, including single-judge disposition, reasonable-doubt finding, and the RICO theory.
We lack jurisdiction to hear most of those arguments, and we affirm the remaining issue.
13658: Mootness: the appeal from a Rule 12(b)(6) §101 ineligibility judgment was dismissed as moot because the settlement's $100 option to add the '043 patent was a token side bet, not a live controversy.
After review, we determine this appeal is moot.
13659: Board jurisdiction over the employee's appeal: no appealable mixed case (no appealable adverse action) and no exhausted individual right of action (IRA) whistleblower claim before OSC, so the Board lacked jurisdiction.
We therefore see no error in the Board's determination that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. May's appeal as a mixed case.
13665: Veterans Court jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7252: whether the 2019 Board remand/reconsideration dismissal was a Board 'decision' reviewable by the Veterans Court; the court found no evident decision on any benefit and did not definitively resolve the question.
Mr. Stiles has not made the double shift needed to show error in the Veterans Court's statutory-jurisdiction ruling.
13670: Jurisdiction under 5 U.S.C. § 7121(f) to review an arbitrator's removal decision for a VA nurse hired under 38 U.S.C. § 7401(1); the court held it lacks jurisdiction and dismissed.
Because we are without jurisdiction to consider the arbitrator's decision, we dismiss Ms. Quillet's petition for lack of jurisdiction.
13677: Scope of the Federal Circuit's limited jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 over the Veterans Court's interpretation of its prior decision and mandate, with the court finding jurisdiction to review that legal question.
We have jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's interpretation of its Hooper 2021 decision.
13678: Board jurisdiction: whether the MSPB had jurisdiction over an appeal of the agency's denial or disqualification of Robinson's VSIP application, where no removal or other enumerated 5 U.S.C. § 7512 action was alleged.
Mr. Robinson points to no persuasive authority supporting his argument that the circumstances here confer Board jurisdiction.
13681: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: no jurisdiction over remaining contentions, including constitutional claims, fact-bound challenges and judicial misconduct allegations.
We lack jurisdiction to consider Mr. Lopez’s remaining contentions, including his purported constitutional claims.
13689: Board jurisdiction over the appeal: the court held the Board lacks jurisdiction because no final OPM decision exists to review and no constructive denial occurred.

We agree the Board lacks jurisdiction because nothing in the record supports the existence of a final decision by OPM for the Board to review and the Board only has jurisdiction over the actions made appealable to it by law.
13694: Jurisdiction over the Veterans Court's application of law to fact: whether the court could review the Veterans Court's determination of whether the January 2008 letter was an adequate NOD (contents of an NOD treated as a factual issue beyond the court's jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292).
Because we lack jurisdiction over Ms. Clark's claims, we dismiss.
13700: Jurisdiction over petition for review: government initially argued untimeliness under the 60-day limit, then withdrew the argument after Harrow held the deadline nonjurisdictional; court found no unfulfilled jurisdictional requirement.
we likewise do not identify any unfulfilled jurisdictional requirement, we address this appeal on the merits.
13734: Board jurisdiction over the individual right of action (IRA) whistleblower appeal; the Board dismissed for lack of jurisdiction and the court affirmed.
We affirm the Board's dismissal of Mr. Defrank's complaint for lack of jurisdiction.
13739: Subject matter jurisdiction under the Tucker Act: the Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction because Serp did not plead a valid contract with the government (no identified contract terms, signatory, or date).
We hold the Court of Federal Claims properly concluded Mr. Serp failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction.
13747: Whether the Court of Federal Claims has Tucker Act jurisdiction over a 26 U.S.C. § 7623(a) whistleblower award claim, i.e., whether § 7623(a) and its implementing regulations are money-mandating. Court held no jurisdiction.
In sum, because § 7623(a) and its implementing regulations are not money-mandating, the Court of Federal Claims correctly concluded that it lacks jurisdiction to review Ms. McCrory's § 7623(a) claim.
13748: Mootness: the appeal from the Board's final written decision was dismissed as moot because the court affirmed in the related Fintiv v. PayPal appeal, which held the same claims of the '386 patent invalid as indefinite.
There is no dispute that our affirmance in the related case compels dismissing as moot this appeal.
13753: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) to review the Veterans Court's denial of a mandamus petition; no legal or constitutional challenge was raised, so the writ issue was dismissed.
We therefore dismiss Mr. Perry's appeal on the writ issue for lack of jurisdiction.
13764: Jurisdiction: the Veterans Court dismissed the appeal because a Board remand order is not a final decision within its jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a). The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction under § 7292 to review the application of law to the facts and dismissed.
Because we lack jurisdiction to consider Mr. Wright's arguments, we dismiss.
13765: Jurisdiction over arguments outside the appeal stream: the Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over the mandamus denial and the December 2024 Board action because those arguments target decisions outside the March 2026 Veterans Court decision under review.
Given that these arguments target decisions outside the present appeal stream, they are beyond the scope of this appeal, and we lack jurisdiction to consider them.
13775: Whether the Board retained jurisdiction over ex parte reexamination after the patent expired; court held the Board has jurisdiction over reexaminations of expired patents.
The Board properly exercised its jurisdiction over this ex parte reexamination.
13777: Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction over most of the plaintiff's claims, which concerned conduct of private individuals, tort claims, and vague allegations against federal agencies.
Accordingly, the Claims Court committed no error in dismissing the complaint in part for lack of jurisdiction.
13799: Jurisdiction: the court analyzed whether the Board's decision granting corrective action was a final order under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) and held the Board's remand-type order was not final, so there was no jurisdiction.
Because the decision of the Board was not final, we lack jurisdiction and therefore dismiss Ms. Trimble's petition.
13801: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) over challenges to the Board's factual findings (that claimant did not set foot in Vietnam or serve in its territorial sea) and the adequacy of its reasons and bases; court held it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed those parts.
We lack jurisdiction to review these issues because they involve "a challenge to a factual determination" and "a challenge to a law . . . as applied to the facts of a particular case."
13802: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2)(B) over the Veterans Court's denial of judicial notice of extra-record evidence; court held it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed that part of the appeal.
We lack jurisdiction to review this issue because it involves "a challenge to a law . . . as applied to the facts of a particular case."
13805: Mootness: appeal of claims overlapping with the companion In re Gesture decision rendered moot, leaving the Board's unpatentability decision for those claims in place.
the appeal of those overlapping claims is rendered moot in light of our companion decision in In re Gesture.
13807: Board jurisdiction over the IPR despite expiration of the '079 patent; Gesture argued the Board lacked jurisdiction, and the court rejected the argument in the companion opinion.

Gesture argues that the Board lacked jurisdiction over this IPR proceeding because the ’079 patent has expired. That issue has been resolved, and rejected, in the separate opinion of Apple Inc. v. Gesture Tech. Partners, LLC
13808: Jurisdiction over breach of contract claims: the Court of Federal Claims lacked Tucker Act jurisdiction because the alleged contracts were with New Mexico agencies, not the federal government.
Accordingly, the Claims Court does not have jurisdiction over Ms. Deweese's breach of contract claims.
13809: Jurisdiction over due process and tort claims: due process clauses do not mandate payment of money under the Tucker Act, and the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over tort claims.
Accordingly, the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over Ms. Deweese's due process and tort claims.
13815: Jurisdiction: the court held it lacks jurisdiction over Garcia's contention that the Board colluded with DFAS in violation of the federal criminal statute, 18 U.S.C. § 242.
We, too, lack jurisdiction over this contention.
13824: Mootness of the appeal as to claims 1, 4, 8, 15, 17 and 19, which were cancelled after a separate IPR found them unpatentable.
This appeal is now moot as to claims 1, 4, 8, 15, 17, and 19, which were cancelled after being found unpatentable in a separate IPR proceeding.
13837: Appellate jurisdiction: whether the appeal was from a final decision where the Court of Federal Claims dismissed the amended complaint but granted leave to amend and later vacated its judgment on reconsideration; court held no final judgment and no jurisdiction.
We conclude that Mr. Bennett did not appeal a final judgment and that we therefore lack jurisdiction, and we dismiss the appeal.
13872: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over the reexamination after the '949 patent expired; resolved and rejected in the companion Apple opinion, so jurisdiction exists.

Finally, Gesture argues that the Board lacked jurisdiction over this reexamination proceeding because the '949 patent has expired. That issue has been resolved, and rejected, in the separate opinion of Apple, No. 23-1501
13873: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court analyzed whether the appeal presented a legal question within its limited jurisdiction and held that the challenges to the flatfoot rating, separate ratings under DC 5284, and the TDIU effective-date issue were factual or application-of-law-to-fact challenges, so there was no jurisdiction.
Because Mr. Regis's appeal does not present issues within our limited jurisdiction, we dismiss.
13879: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over the USERRA claim; the court held the employee failed to nonfrivolously allege that his uniformed service was a substantial or motivating factor in the denial of employment, so the appeal was properly dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
We therefore conclude that the Board did not err in determining that Vindiola had not alleged a USERRA claim sufficient to confer jurisdiction on the Board.
13880: Board's jurisdiction over McCloud's individual right of action (IRA) appeal: retaliation for filing EEO complaints falls under 2302(b)(9)(A)(ii) and is not redressable in an IRA appeal, so the Board lacked jurisdiction and the dismissal was affirmed.

13881: Jurisdiction over the AJ's denial of sanctions for DHS's untimely handling of the mixed-case discrimination claims; court dismissed that portion because the sanctions issue is intertwined with the abandoned discrimination claims.
Consequently, we dismiss for lack of jurisdiction the portion of Mr. Jadue's appeal challenging the denial of his request for sanctions.
13888: Scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: review limited to interpretation of the regulation, not the Board's factual finding about the basis for the March 2016 grant

13897: Board's jurisdiction over a Postal Service employee's appeal of a reduction in grade. The court held the Board lacked jurisdiction because Ramirez was neither a preference-eligible employee nor a supervisor, manager, or personnel worker with one year of continuous service under 39 U.S.C. 1005(a) and 5 U.S.C. 7511(a)(1).
The Board therefore properly determined that Mr. Ramirez does not qualify as an employee with a right to appeal to the Board under 5 U.S.C. § 7511(a)(1).
13902: Appellate jurisdiction/finality: whether the Veterans Court's partial remand decision is sufficiently final for Federal Circuit review under Williams v. Principi; appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction
The Veterans Court's decision is thus not sufficiently final for purposes of our review. We dismiss the appeal.
13912: Jurisdiction over the IRA appeal: whether the Board had jurisdiction, decided under the nonfrivolous-allegation standard; court affirmed dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
we affirm the Board's dismissal of her IRA appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
13922: Jurisdiction over VA's challenge that Baker's arguments contest a factual finding outside the court's review under 38 U.S.C. § 7292; court rejected it
The VA frames Ms. Baker's arguments as contesting a factual finding over which we lack jurisdiction. We do not agree.
13940: Whether claims were properly before the Veterans Court: the court held that the apportionment and unadjudicated service-connection claims were not addressed by the Board and so were not properly before the Veterans Court, and that the counsel request was not properly before it because no appeal was pending.

To the extent that he seeks to raise the issue of the denial of apportionment of his disability compensation to his mother or his claims for service connection for conditions other than tinnitus, those claims have not been addressed by the Board of Veterans' Appeals and thus were not properly before the Veterans Court.
13943: Jurisdiction over appeal of Veterans Court denial of reconsideration on a waiver finding; court held 38 U.S.C. §7292 does not permit review of the Veterans Court's waiver determination and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Because we lack jurisdiction, we must dismiss.
13947: Jurisdiction: whether the court has jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 to review the Veterans Court's denial of mandamus, given that the veteran raised no non-frivolous legal question.
We thus lack jurisdiction to consider his arguments.
13961: Tucker Act jurisdiction of the Court of Federal Claims over the alleged education-services contract; the court reversed the jurisdictional dismissal, finding jurisdiction.
We conclude that the Claims Court had jurisdiction pursuant to the Tucker Act over the agreement alleged here. The jurisdictional dismissal must be reversed.
13966: Mootness and case-or-controversy: the court held the government's appeal of the Claims Court's Solicitation I rulings moot and declined to apply the capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception. Dismissal leaves the Claims Court's ruling for the protester in place.
This case is moot because there is no longer a live issue.
13970: Subject-matter jurisdiction over claims for damages under I.R.C. § 7433 and for tortious and criminal conduct: no Tucker Act jurisdiction over tort or criminal claims, and § 7433 damages lie exclusively in district court.
With respect to the claims of tortious and criminal conduct, we affirm the dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
13973: Board jurisdiction over Postal Service removal appeal: whether Anderson qualified under PEARA as preference-eligible or supervisory/management employee with Board appeal rights; Board lacked jurisdiction and dismissal affirmed
Because Ms. Anderson has not shown that she qualified as an employee with Board appeal rights, the Board correctly dismissed her appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
13983: Whether the Court of Federal Claims had subject matter jurisdiction over a refund claim for payments made under a criminal sentence, including pardon power, implied contract, illegal exaction, and money-mandating provisions theories; the court held it lacked jurisdiction.
Here, Mr. Boultbee fails to establish a ground to invoke the Claims Court's limited jurisdiction.
13986: Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2): the court held it lacked jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's application of law to fact, including its forfeiture finding, and dismissed the appeal.
Because Mr. Rorie's arguments on appeal challenge the Veteran's Court's application of law to fact, we dismiss this appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
13996: Jurisdiction: the court held it is statutorily barred under 5 U.S.C. § 8461(d) from reviewing the factual determination underlying OPM's denial of physical disability retirement.
We are therefore statutorily barred from considering this argument because it is a request to reconsider a factual matter relating to OPM's determination that Chafin was not physically disabled.
14000: Jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held the appeal fell outside its limited jurisdiction because the Veterans Court decision did not involve the validity or interpretation of a statute or regulation, the duty-to-assist and application-of-law-to-fact arguments were factual or fact-bound, and no constitutional issue was genuinely raised.
Mr. Clegg's appeal, however, falls outside our limited jurisdiction over appeals from a Veterans Court decision.
14001: Trial court's jurisdiction over breach of settlement contract claims; court agreed the trial court had jurisdiction over the contract claims despite a conflicting statement
We agree with the trial court's initial conclusion that it had jurisdiction.
14003: Fraudulent inducement claim is a tort outside the CFC's jurisdiction because it predates the settlement contract; merits vacated and dismissal treated as jurisdictional
The trial court therefore should have held that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Strong's fraudulent inducement claim.
14007: Lack of appellate jurisdiction over arguments on the reconsideration denial because no amended notice of appeal was filed
Since he did not, we lack jurisdiction to consider these arguments and therefore dismiss them.
14010: Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction over a USPS employee's removal appeal; petitioner failed to allege facts showing preference-eligible status or a supervisory/managerial or personnel-work position with one year of service.
Because Ms. Bedoya has not alleged or provided evidence of a basis for jurisdiction, we affirm the Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
14016: Jurisdiction: Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Counts I, II, III-VII, IX and XI because the cited statutes (Privacy Act, 10 U.S.C. 1557, MWPA) are not money-mandating.
As such, we agree that the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over Count I, and thus affirm the trial court's decision to dismiss Count I.
14021: Board jurisdiction: Board lacked jurisdiction to consider a performance rating as an independent basis for reversal because performance ratings are not appealable actions.
the Board lacked jurisdiction to consider this issue.
14022: Court's jurisdiction over FOIA challenge: Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over the denial or delay of Agboke's FOIA request, which belongs in district court.
We agree with the agency that this Court lacks jurisdiction to hear Agboke's challenge to the response to his FOIA request.
14026: Mootness of the mandamus petition: the court held the petition was not moot when filed in 2022, and remanded to the Veterans Court to consider in the first instance whether a mootness exception applies after the February 2023 letter.

Our conclusion that Mr. Hamill's 2021 VA decision could not implicitly deny his character of discharge claim necessarily means his petition to the Veterans Court, which sought to compel adjudication, was not moot when it was filed in 2022.
14030: Federal Circuit jurisdiction over appeal from Veterans Court dismissal for lack of jurisdiction; court found no jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. 7292 because no legal, constitutional, or discernible challenge was presented.
We thus have no jurisdiction over Ms. Scotto's appeal.
14041: Jurisdiction over the EAJA travel-expense ruling: the court found jurisdiction because the Veterans Court's decision turned on interpretation of 5 U.S.C. § 504 and Richlin.
We accordingly have jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's decision to the extent that it relied upon a legal interpretation of a statute.
14042: No jurisdiction over EAJA claims for research and writing, internet service, and printing expenses because they rest on application of law to fact.
We do not have jurisdiction as to Mr. Delano's claims for research and writing, internet service, and printing expenses because his claims are based on an application of law to fact.
14045: Appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292: the court held it lacked jurisdiction because the appeal challenged factual determinations (relatedness of disabilities) and mere application of regulations to facts, with no constitutional challenge presented.
We lack jurisdiction over this appeal because Mr. Cook challenges factual determinations and does not present a constitutional challenge.
14063: Lack of Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction over Tomko's defamation and other tort claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1).
Meanwhile, the defamation claims are tort claims over which the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction.
14064: Mootness: after the Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's unpatentability decisions on all asserted patents, the ITC investigation was moot, so the Commission's decision was vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss.
Now that we have affirmed the Board's finding of unpatentability for each Asserted Patent, the Commission's investigation is moot.
14072: Board jurisdiction: due process claims raised by the employee fall outside the Board's limited review in an IRA appeal, so the Board lacked jurisdiction over them.
these arguments would not have been within the Board's jurisdiction.
14092: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's refusal to consider a substantive challenge to the VA's 0% rating schedule under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a) and Wingard; the court held it lacks jurisdiction and dismissed.

14112: Appeal No. 23-1721 from the anticipation determination in IPR2021-00721 dismissed as moot in light of the affirmance on obviousness.
